# .bin File Format

> Documentation for the .bin file format used to release smaller applications

## Overview

[Section titled “Overview”](#overview)

The `.bin` file format is used to release applications similar to a shellcode payload or a rom dump. It have limits on the program size but should be suited for small to medium programs and games.

This format allows the specification of a load address and provides flexibility for different loading scenarios.

## History

[Section titled “History”](#history)

The `.bin` file format was introduced as a solution to a bug identified in the `.elf` loader for `.hhk` files. The initial loader utilized the `getaddress` function, which incorrectly assumed it could access the entire file. However, this was problematic for larger files that might be split across different sections of flash memory. As a result, when dealing with files larger than a few kilobytes, the loader would often fail because it couldn’t access the necessary parts of the file.

To address this, the `.bin` format was developed with the following considerations:

* **Direct File Access**: The new design used file read functions instead of directly accessing flash memory, ensuring proper handling of files stored in non-contiguous blocks.

* **Flexible Execution**: The goal was to allow both plain machine code and `.bin` files to be loaded and executed. If a file contains only machine code, it should still work without needing any specific headers. The optional load address allows for custom loading of `.bin` files while maintaining backward compatibility.

### Loader Behavior

[Section titled “Loader Behavior”](#loader-behavior)

The loader checks if the load address starts with `0x8C`. If it does, it treats it as a load address; otherwise, it assumes the file contains raw executable code. This approach, while effective, carries some risk: there’s a possibility that a machine code instruction could inadvertently contain `0x8C`, leading to potential crashes.

The implementation was aimed to support various combinations of loaders and file types:

* Simple loaders that copy everything to `0x8CFF0000` and execute it.
* Plain assembly files executed by both simple loaders and the custom loader.
* `.bin` files with and without load addresses or program descriptions.

You can check the [Bin Loader source code on GitHub](https://github.com/SnailMath/hollyhock-2/blob/master/launcher/bins.cpp#L113)

## File Structure

[Section titled “File Structure”](#file-structure)

The `.bin` file consists of a header followed by the executable code. The header provides essential information for loading and executing the application.

### Header Details

[Section titled “Header Details”](#header-details)

| Offset | Bytes    | Description                                                                 |
| ------ | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| 00     | 2        | `D0 01` - Load the address from 0x08                                        |
| 02     | 2        | `40 2B` - Jump to that address                                              |
| 04     | 2        | `00 09` - NOP (No Operation) because the last instruction is a delayed jump |
| 06     | 2        | Unused - reserved for future releases                                       |
| 08     | 4        | Entry point (loaded by the code at offset 00)                               |
| 0C     | 4        | Load address (used by the loader, must start with `8C`)                     |
| 10     | Variable | Name, Description, Author, Version, Null Terminated                         |

### Compatibility

[Section titled “Compatibility”](#compatibility)

For compatibility reasons, if the load address at offset `0x0C` does not start with `8C`, the default load address is used. Additionally, if the name does not start with an ASCII character, it is also ignored. This ensures that a plain executable code file can also be used without the header information being mandatory.

## Usage

[Section titled “Usage”](#usage)

When a `.bin` file is loaded, the loader reads the header to determine the entry point and load address. The executable code is then loaded into memory at the specified address, and execution begins from the entry point.

### Example

[Section titled “Example”](#example)

Here’s an example of how the .bin file might look:

```plaintext
Offset | Hex Data                 | Description
-------|--------------------------|------------------------------------------------
00     | D0 01                    | Load address from 0x08
02     | 40 2B                    | Jump to the address loaded from 0x08
04     | 00 09                    | NOP (delayed jump)
06     | 00 09                    | Unused
08     | 8C FF 00 9A              | Entry point
0C     | 8C FF 00 00              | Load address
10     | 54 75 74 6F 00           | "Tuto" (Name)
15     | 64 65 73 63 00           | "desc" (Description)
1A     | 61 75 74 68 6F 72 00     | "author" (Author)
```

Here, the sample application “Tuto” with the description “desc” and author “author” is loaded at the address `8C FF 00 00`, and execution begins at the entry point `8C FF 00 9A`.

It would appear as such like the following launcher :

![Sample HHK launcher screenshot](/wiki/img/gui/hhk_demo.png)

# Adding Your Calculator to MyCalcs

> User guide for registering your calculator model on MyCalcs platform

This guide will walk you through the process of registering your calculator on MyCalcs.

Why register ?

Adding your calculator serial number to MyCalcs helps us understand hardware changes and provide updates to newer models faster.

### Access the Platform

[Section titled “Access the Platform”](#access-the-platform)

Go to <https://my.calcs.quest/?ref=402> and select **“Sign up”** from the top right corner.

### Create an Account

[Section titled “Create an Account”](#create-an-account)

Fill in the registration form with:

* Username
* Password
* Email address

Check **“Accept the ToS”** and click **“Sign up”**.

### Login to Your Account

[Section titled “Login to Your Account”](#login-to-your-account)

After successful registration, you should see the message: *“Note: Signup successful. You can now log in.”*

Click **“Log in”** at the top and enter your credentials.

### Access Your Profile

[Section titled “Access Your Profile”](#access-your-profile)

Click on your username in the top bar and select **“Go to your profile”**.

### Add Your Calculator

[Section titled “Add Your Calculator”](#add-your-calculator)

Click the **“Add a new calculator”** button.

### Fill Calculator Information

[Section titled “Fill Calculator Information”](#fill-calculator-information)

In the popup window, provide the following information:

**Required Fields:**

* **Brand:** Casio
* **Model:** cp400 (or cg500 or cp400+E)
* **Serial:** Located next to the batteries on your calculator

**Additional Information:**

* **SW. version(s):** Include the ABS version (2012 or 2022) and your HollyHock version (found in the main menu: Menu > Version)
* **Acquisition date:** When you purchased the calculator
* **Photo URL:** Link to an image hosted on a service like <https://imgbb.com>
* **Condition:** New or used
* **Comment:** Any interesting stories or special features about your calculator

Click **“Add calculator”** to complete the process.

Thanks !

# Memory Mapping

> Internal memory mapping of the fx-CP400

## Mapping Table

[Section titled “Mapping Table”](#mapping-table)

| Region        | Start         | End           | Size      | Notes                             |
| ------------- | ------------- | ------------- | --------- | --------------------------------- |
| Boot ROM      | `0x0000_0000` | -             | -         | Initial boot code                 |
| Main RAM      | `0x8C00_0000` | `0x8CFF_FFFF` | 16 MB     | OS + apps + heap                  |
| Cached ROM    | `0x8000_0000` | `0x81FF_FFFF` | 512 MB    | Cached access                     |
| MCS FS        | `0x8E00_0000` | -             | -         | Filesystem (avoid overwriting!)   |
| Uncached ROM  | `0xA000_0000` | `0xA1FF_FFFF` | 512 MB    | Direct, no cache                  |
| CPG           | `0xA415_0000` | `0xA415_FFFF` | 64 KB     | Clock control                     |
| Touch?        | `0xA405_0100` | -             | -         | Touch register at `0xA405_01F3`   |
| Display DMAC  | `0xB400_0000` | -             | -         | Display DMA controller            |
| **XRAM**      | `0xE500_7000` | `0xE500_9000` | **8 KB**  | Fast data RAM (Bank 1)            |
| **YRAM**      | `0xE501_7000` | `0xE501_9000` | **8 KB**  | Fast data RAM (Bank 2)            |
| **IL Memory** | `0xE520_0000` | `0xE520_4000` | **16 KB** | Fast instruction RAM              |
| Direct I/O    | `0xFEC0_0000` | `0xFEFF_FFFF` | 4 MB      | Hardware registers                |
| **RS Memory** | `0xFD80_0000` | `0xFD80_07FF` | **2 KB**  | CRITICAL. Retained during standby |

***

Here’s some informations gathered about the mapping :

* boot rom is at `0x0000_0000`, it’s taken from the first part of the flashed rom

* bootloader is at `0x0000_0300` with the `LV777` then `CASIOABS` at `0x0000_3380`

* Clock Pulse Generator (CPG) is at `0xA415_0000` to `0xA415_FFFF`

* `0xA405_0100` may be the touchscreen, where `0xA405_01F3` changes when screen it touched

* RAM is `0x8c00_0000` to `0x8cff_ffff`

* MCS starts at `0x8e00_0000`

* Cached ROM is `0x8000_0000` to `0x81ff_ffff`

* Uncached ROM is `0xa000_0000` to `0xa1ff_ffff`

* Display DMAC start at `0xb400_0000`

* There are some “direct Io” from `0xFEC0_0000` to `0xFEFF_FFFF`

## RAM

[Section titled “RAM”](#ram)

When [loading a .bin program](https://github.com/SnailMath/hollyhock-2/blob/master/launcher/bins.cpp#L178), it is copied at `0x8cff_0000` and the PC jump to this offset

> For hollyhock, we usually use the end of the ram, that space is usually occupied by the mcs file system, but if it’s not fully full, then it should work. Just note that the hollyhock launcher is running from ram, so it can’t overwrite itself…`8C00_0000` to `8CFF_FFFF` is ram, we use [`8CFE_0000`](https://github.com/SnailMath/hollyhock-2/blob/master/patches/file_loader/file_loader.s#L134) for the launcher (from the run.bin file) and [`8CFF_0000`](https://github.com/SnailMath/hollyhock-2/blob/master/launcher/bins.cpp#L178) for [programs](https://github.com/TheRainbowPhoenix/CPAppTemplate/blob/main/linker_bin.ld#L4), just look at the launcher how big it is, you can squeeze out a bit if you start your program at `8CFE_8000`…

## Triple Screen Buffer

[Section titled “Triple Screen Buffer”](#triple-screen-buffer)

A large, **continuous** memory area is dynamically available on the RAM. Though it is allocated dynamically, a static pointer to it can be found at the address `0x8c2233a0` (`MenuIcons::m_gpBitmap`).

You can safely use this area for continuous data structure, such as dynamically loaded code, non-persistent data, or huge data structures. This provides over 560 kB of fixed buffer space, which is excellent for loading large programs in an environment without a MMU (Memory Management Unit).

![Trible Screen Buffer](/wiki/img/triple_screen.png)

# Drawing Shapes

> Creating Your First App - Drawing on the Classpad screen

# Drawing Shapes on Your Classpad Calculator

[Section titled “Drawing Shapes on Your Classpad Calculator”](#drawing-shapes-on-your-classpad-calculator)

This tutorial will guide you through drawing various shapes on your Classpad calculator screen using C++. We’ll build upon the “Hello World” app you created earlier.

## Prerequisites

[Section titled “Prerequisites”](#prerequisites)

Make sure you have completed the [Hello World tutorial](/wiki/examples/hello-world/) before proceeding. Your `main.cpp` file should look similar to the final code from that tutorial.

## Step 1: Understanding the Drawing Functions

[Section titled “Step 1: Understanding the Drawing Functions”](#step-1-understanding-the-drawing-functions)

Before we start drawing, let’s understand the key functions available for creating shapes:

1. **`setPixel(x, y, color)`** - Draws a single pixel at coordinates (x, y)
2. **`line(x1, y1, x2, y2, color)`** - Draws a line between two points
3. **`triangle(x0, y0, x1, y1, x2, y2, colorFill, colorLine)`** - Draws a filled triangle with outline
4. **`fillScreen(color)`** - Fills the entire screen with a color

For more details about them, please [check the reference](/wiki/reference/calc/calc/)

## Step 2: Setting Up Your Canvas

[Section titled “Step 2: Setting Up Your Canvas”](#step-2-setting-up-your-canvas)

Start with the basic app structure from the Hello World tutorial. Replace the text drawing code with shape drawing code:

```cpp
#include <appdef.hpp>
#include <sdk/calc/calc.hpp>
#include <sdk/os/lcd.hpp>
#include <sdk/os/debug.hpp>


APP_NAME("Shape Drawing")
APP_DESCRIPTION("Drawing various shapes")
APP_AUTHOR("Your Name")
APP_VERSION("1.0.0")


extern "C"
void main() {
    calcInit(); // Initialize the screen


    // Clear screen with black background
    fillScreen(color(0, 0, 0));


    /* TODO: Your shape drawing code goes here ... */


    calcEnd(); // Restore the screen to the initial state
}
```

## Step 3: Drawing Pixels

[Section titled “Step 3: Drawing Pixels”](#step-3-drawing-pixels)

Let’s start with the most basic element - individual pixels. Add this code where the TODO comment is:

```cpp
// Draw a pattern of pixels
for (int i = 0; i < 100; i += 10) {
    setPixel(50 + i, 50, color(255, 255, 255)); // White pixels
    setPixel(50, 50 + i, color(255, 0, 0));     // Red pixels
}
```

This creates two lines of pixels - one horizontal and one vertical.

## Step 4: Drawing Lines

[Section titled “Step 4: Drawing Lines”](#step-4-drawing-lines)

Now let’s draw some lines using the `line()` function:

```cpp
// Draw various lines
line(10, 10, 100, 100, color(255, 0, 0));     // Red diagonal line
line(150, 50, 250, 50, color(0, 255, 0));     // Green horizontal line
line(200, 100, 200, 200, color(0, 0, 255));   // Blue vertical line
line(50, 150, 250, 200, 0b1111100000000000);  // Line using 565 color format
```

Lines can be drawn using either RGB color values or the 565 color format.

## Step 5: Drawing Triangles

[Section titled “Step 5: Drawing Triangles”](#step-5-drawing-triangles)

Triangles are more complex shapes that can be filled and outlined:

```cpp
// Draw filled triangles
triangle(30, 30, 80, 30, 55, 80, color(255, 255, 0), color(255, 0, 255));
//           P0      P1      P2      Fill Color        Line Color


// Draw another triangle
triangle(100, 150, 200, 150, 150, 250, color(0, 255, 255), color(255, 255, 255));
```

Each triangle requires three points (P0, P1, P2) and two colors - one for filling and one for the outline.

## Step 6: Creating Color Patterns

[Section titled “Step 6: Creating Color Patterns”](#step-6-creating-color-patterns)

Let’s create a colorful pattern using nested loops:

```cpp
// Draw a colorful rectangle using pixels
for (int x = 0; x < 100; x++) {
    for (int y = 0; y < 100; y++) {
        setPixel(100 + x, 300 + y, color(x * 2, y * 2, 100));
    }
}
```

This creates a 100x100 pixel rectangle with a color gradient.

## Step 7: Updating the Screen

[Section titled “Step 7: Updating the Screen”](#step-7-updating-the-screen)

After drawing all your shapes, you need to refresh the screen to see them:

```cpp
LCD_Refresh(); // Update the screen to show all drawn shapes
```

## Step 8: Adding User Interaction

[Section titled “Step 8: Adding User Interaction”](#step-8-adding-user-interaction)

To keep your app running until the user exits, add the key input loop:

```cpp
// Wait for user to press CLEAR key to exit
while(true) {
    uint32_t key1, key2;
    getKey(&key1, &key2);
    if(testKey(key1, key2, KEY_CLEAR)) {
        break;
    }
}
```

## Complete Example Code

[Section titled “Complete Example Code”](#complete-example-code)

Here’s the complete code for your shape drawing app:

```cpp
#include <appdef.hpp>
#include <sdk/calc/calc.hpp>
#include <sdk/os/lcd.hpp>
#include <sdk/os/debug.hpp>


APP_NAME("Shape Drawing")
APP_DESCRIPTION("Drawing various shapes")
APP_AUTHOR("Your Name")
APP_VERSION("1.0.0")


extern "C"
void main() {
    calcInit(); // Initialize the screen


    // Clear screen with black background
    fillScreen(color(0, 0, 0));


    // Draw individual pixels
    for (int i = 0; i < 100; i += 10) {
        setPixel(50 + i, 50, color(255, 255, 255)); // White pixels
        setPixel(50, 50 + i, color(255, 0, 0));     // Red pixels
    }


    // Draw various lines
    line(10, 10, 100, 100, color(255, 0, 0));     // Red diagonal line
    line(150, 50, 250, 50, color(0, 255, 0));     // Green horizontal line
    line(200, 100, 200, 200, color(0, 0, 255));   // Blue vertical line
    line(50, 150, 250, 200, 0b1111100000000000);  // Line using 565 color format


    // Draw filled triangles
    triangle(30, 30, 80, 30, 55, 80, color(255, 255, 0), color(255, 0, 255));
    triangle(100, 150, 200, 150, 150, 250, color(0, 255, 255), color(255, 255, 255));


    // Draw a colorful rectangle using pixels
    for (int x = 0; x < 100; x++) {
        for (int y = 0; y < 100; y++) {
            setPixel(100 + x, 300 + y, color(x * 2, y * 2, 100));
        }
    }


    // Update the screen to show all drawn shapes
    LCD_Refresh();


    // Wait for user to press CLEAR key to exit
    while(true) {
        uint32_t key1, key2;
        getKey(&key1, &key2);
        if(testKey(key1, key2, KEY_CLEAR)) {
            break;
        }
    }


    calcEnd(); // Restore the screen to the initial state
}
```

## Next Steps

[Section titled “Next Steps”](#next-steps)

Congratulations! You’ve learned how to draw various shapes on your Classpad !

Now that you know how to draw shapes, try:

* Creating more complex patterns
* Drawing multiple shapes in different colors
* Making interactive drawings that respond to key presses
* Creating simple games using these drawing functions

# Hello World

> Creating Your First App - Hello World for the Classpad

This tutorial will guide you through creating a simple “Hello World” app for your Classpad calculator using C++. Even if you’re new to C development, we’ll take it step by step.

## Step 1: Empty base

[Section titled “Step 1: Empty base”](#step-1-empty-base)

Start with the [“Application Template”](/wiki/getting-started/introduction/#instant-coding-using-online-codespace).

Go to your codespace and open the “**main.cpp**” file. Delete all of its content (Ctrl-a → Delete) and start by adding only the needed imports :

```c++
#include <appdef.hpp>
#include <sdk/calc/calc.hpp>
#include <sdk/os/lcd.hpp>
#include <sdk/os/debug.hpp>
```

Here, we include essential files that provide functionalities for creating apps on the Classpad calculator. Let’s break down what each import does:

* `<appdef.hpp>`: This file helps **define essential properties** of your app, such as its **name**, **description**, author, and version. Think of it as setting up the basic information for your project, as they will **appear on the launcher menu** as it.
* `<sdk/calc/calc.hpp>`: This file includes functions and settings related to the Classpad calculator itself, like initializing and ending the calculator environment
* `<sdk/os/lcd.hpp>`: The LCD (Liquid Crystal Display) file is crucial for interacting with the calculator’s screen. It provides functions for refreshing the display and setting pixel colors.
* `<sdk/os/debug.hpp>`: The debug file assists in debugging your code by offering functions for printing messages and setting cursor positions on the calculator screen.

Now, let’s move on to the next step and start building your “Hello World” app!

Psst, lost ?

You can peek at [the end section](#final-code) the final code for the `main.cpp`, or at any time **[💬 Join our Discord community](https://discord.gg/knpcNJTzpd)** to ask for help !

## Step 2: Set Up Your App Information

[Section titled “Step 2: Set Up Your App Information”](#step-2-set-up-your-app-information)

Start by filling in some basic information about your app. Open the code and look for the following lines:

```c++
APP_NAME("Hello World")
APP_DESCRIPTION("App that says hello")
APP_AUTHOR("You")
APP_VERSION("1.0.0")
```

Here, you can customize your app’s name, description, author, and version. This **information is optional** but helps you keep track of your project and **understand** what it is doing on the **launcher menu**.

## Step 3: Writing the Main C++ Function

[Section titled “Step 3: Writing the Main C++ Function”](#step-3-writing-the-main-c-function)

Now, let’s dive into the heart of your app - the `main()` function. In C++, every program starts executing from a function called `main()`. Think of it as the command center of your code. When you run your app, the instructions inside `main()` are carried out one by one.

```c++
extern "C"
void main() {
  /* TODO: Your code goes here ... */
}
```

Here’s a simple breakdown:

* `extern "C"`: This is a technicality that ensures compatibility between C and C++ code. For now, you can consider it a standard part of starting a C++ program.

* `void main() { /* ... */ }`: This is the beginning of your program. The void here means that the main() function doesn’t return any value.

Inside the curly braces `{ /* ... */ }`, you’ll put the instructions that make up your app. It’s like a recipe; the computer follows these steps when you run your program.

## Step 4: The Calculator Environment

[Section titled “Step 4: The Calculator Environment”](#step-4-the-calculator-environment)

Now, let’s understand two important functions: `calcInit()` and `calcEnd()`. These functions manage the calculator environment.

* `calcInit()`: This function initializes the calculator environment, preparing it for your app. It’s like turning on the lights and getting everything ready before your program starts.

* `calcEnd()`: This function restores the calculator to its initial state after your program finishes. It’s like cleaning up and turning off the lights when you’re done.

Place this code inside the backets of the `main()` function :

```c++
    calcInit(); // Initialize the screen


    /* TODO: Your code goes here ... */


    calcEnd(); // Restore the screen to the initial state
```

These functions ensure your app interacts smoothly with the calculator without leaving any mess behind. Now you’re ready to add your “Hello World” message to the calculator screen!

## Step 5: Adding Color with fillScreen()

[Section titled “Step 5: Adding Color with fillScreen()”](#step-5-adding-color-with-fillscreen)

Now, let’s add some color to your app using fillScreen(color(0,0,0)). In simple terms, this function fills the calculator screen with a specified color. The color(0,0,0) corresponds to the RGB values for red, green, and blue, respectively. Here, it’s set to black.

```c++
    fillScreen(color(0,0,0)); // Fill the screen with a black color (Red, Green, Blue)


    /* TODO: Your code goes here ... */
```

Think of it as setting the background of your app. You can change these values to experiment with different colors.

## Step 6: Drawing Text on the Screen Buffer

[Section titled “Step 6: Drawing Text on the Screen Buffer”](#step-6-drawing-text-on-the-screen-buffer)

Now, let’s position your “Hello World” message on the screen using Debug\_SetCursorPosition(). The function takes the X and Y coordinates as parameters, where each unit is 12 pixels horizontally (X) and 24 pixels vertically (Y).

```c++
Debug_SetCursorPosition(6,2); // Set the position to  x=6, y=2 (72px, 48px)
Debug_PrintString("Hello World !",0);
```

* `Debug_SetCursorPosition(6,2)`: This sets the position cursor where your text will be drawn. The coordinates (6, 2) translate to (x=72px, y=12px) on the actual screen as the font size is 6x12.

* `Debug_PrintString("Hello World !",0)`: This draws the text “Hello World !” on the screen buffer, but won’t display it right now.

Here, your message will appear at (72px, 12px) on the screen after the next step. Feel free to adjust the coordinates to place your text where you want.

Step 7: Updating the Screen with LCD\_Refresh()

After making changes to the screen buffer, you need to tell the calculator to show those changes. Think of it like taking a snapshot of your changes and making them visible.

```c++
LCD_Refresh(); // Update the screen to show the changes
```

This is the final touch to ensure your “Hello World” message is displayed as intended.

## Step 8: Waiting for User Input

[Section titled “Step 8: Waiting for User Input”](#step-8-waiting-for-user-input)

Now, your app would run and disappear quickly. The last part ensures your message stays until the user is ready to exit. It waits for any key to be pressed:

```c++
while(true){
    uint32_t key1, key2;    // First create variables
    getKey(&key1, &key2);    // then read the keys
    if(testKey(key1, key2, KEY_CLEAR)){ // Use testKey() to test if a specific key is pressed
        break;
    }
}
```

It creates a loop that keeps running until a key is pressed, making sure your “Hello World” message stays on the screen until the user is ready. Don’t worry if it’s a bit difficult to understand, as the next tutorial will dive into key inputs !

## Step 9: Build and install the app

[Section titled “Step 9: Build and install the app”](#step-9-build-and-install-the-app)

![Right click on the "main.cpp" and open in terminal](/wiki/img/tutorials/main-open-in-term.png)

Inside the terminal, enter the following text : `make bin`

On the file tree, you should see a newly created file named “**app\_template.bin**”. You can right click it and **download** it to your desktop.

Now, **plug your calculator** and put this file on the **root folder of the calculator** (not the *Autoimport*, the very **root folder that opens**).

Finally, unplug your calculator and on the *menu → System → Hollyhock-2 Launcher* search for the “**Hello World**” app and launch it.

You should see something like this :

![Final preview of what should be visible on the calculator](/wiki/img/hello-world-final.png)

**Congratulations**! You’ve successfully added color, positioned text, and made your first app interactive. Now, you can run your code and see your “Hello World” message on your Classpad!

## Final code

[Section titled “Final code”](#final-code)

```c++
#include <appdef.hpp>
#include <sdk/calc/calc.hpp>
#include <sdk/os/lcd.hpp>
#include <sdk/os/debug.hpp>


/*
 * Fill this section in with some information about your app.
 * All fields are optional - so if you don't need one, take it out.
 */
APP_NAME("Hello World")
APP_DESCRIPTION("App that says hello")
APP_AUTHOR("You")
APP_VERSION("1.0.0")


extern "C"
void main() {
  calcInit(); // Initialize the screen


  //Example for fillScreen(color);
  fillScreen(color(0,0,0)); // Red, Green, Blue


  Debug_SetCursorPosition(6,2);
  Debug_PrintString("Hello World !",0);


  //use this command to actually update the screen
  LCD_Refresh();


  // Wait for any key to be pressed. Used to not exit right after showing the text. Ingore this for now
  while(true){
    uint32_t key1, key2;  // First create variables
    getKey(&key1, &key2);  // then read the keys
    if(testKey(key1, key2, KEY_CLEAR)){ // Use testKey() to test if a specific key is pressed
      break;
    }
  }


  calcEnd(); //restore the screen to initial state
}
```

# Working with the keyboard

> Tutorial on how to work with the keyboard on the Classpad

This tutorial will guide you through handling keyboard input on your Classpad calculator using C++. Even if you’re new to C development, we’ll take it step by step.

## Step 1: Empty base

[Section titled “Step 1: Empty base”](#step-1-empty-base)

Start with the [“Application Template”](/wiki/getting-started/introduction/#instant-coding-using-online-codespace).

Go to your codespace and open the `main.cpp` file. Ensure it have the needed imports :

```c++
#include <appdef.hpp>
#include <sdk/calc/calc.hpp>
#include <sdk/os/input.hpp>
#include <sdk/os/lcd.hpp>
#include <sdk/os/debug.hpp>
```

Here, we’ll need:

* `<appdef.hpp>`: Defines app properties like name and version
* [`<sdk/calc/calc.hpp>`](/wiki/reference/calc/calc/) to manage the calculator environment and graphics
* [`<sdk/os/input.hpp>`](/wiki/reference/os/input/) to manage the key events
* [`<sdk/os/lcd.hpp>`](/wiki/reference/os/lcd/) to draw on the screen
* [`<sdk/os/debug.hpp>`](/wiki/reference/os/debug/) to do `Debug_Printf` when debugging your application

## Step 2: Set Up Your App Information

[Section titled “Step 2: Set Up Your App Information”](#step-2-set-up-your-app-information)

Add your app’s basic information:

```c++
APP_NAME("TouchRectangle")
APP_DESCRIPTION("Move a rectangle based on touch and key input.")
APP_AUTHOR("Your Name")
APP_VERSION("1.0.0")
```

## Step 3: Define Constants and Variables

[Section titled “Step 3: Define Constants and Variables”](#step-3-define-constants-and-variables)

Add constants for colors, rectangle size, and movement:

```c++
#define COLOR_BACKGROUND RGB_TO_RGB565(0, 0, 0)
#define COLOR_RECTANGLE RGB_TO_RGB565(0x1F, 0, 0)


#define RECT_SIZE 20
#define MOVE_STEP 5


extern uint16_t *vram;
int lcdWidth, lcdHeight;
int rectX, rectY;
```

These constants define:

* `COLOR_BACKGROUND`: Black background color
* `COLOR_RECTANGLE`: Red rectangle color
* `RECT_SIZE`: Size of the rectangle in pixels
* `MOVE_STEP`: How many pixels to move with each key press

## Step 4: Create Drawing Functions

[Section titled “Step 4: Create Drawing Functions”](#step-4-create-drawing-functions)

Create functions to draw the rectangle and update the screen:

```c++
void drawRectangle(int x, int y, uint16_t color) {
  for (int i = x; i < x + RECT_SIZE; ++i) {
    for (int j = y; j < y + RECT_SIZE; ++j) {
      if (i >= 0 && i < lcdWidth && j >= 0 && j < lcdHeight) {
        vram[i + (j + 24) * lcdWidth] = color;
      }
    }
  }
}


void draw() {
  LCD_ClearScreen();
  drawRectangle(rectX, rectY, COLOR_RECTANGLE);
  LCD_Refresh();
}
```

The `drawRectangle` function draws a filled rectangle at position (x, y) with the specified color. The `draw` function clears the screen, draws the rectangle, and refreshes the display.

## Step 5: Initialize the App

[Section titled “Step 5: Initialize the App”](#step-5-initialize-the-app)

Set up the main function with initialization code:

```c++
extern "C"
void main() {
  LCD_VRAMBackup();
  vram = LCD_GetVRAMAddress();
  LCD_GetSize(&lcdWidth, &lcdHeight);


  rectX = lcdWidth / 2 - RECT_SIZE / 2;
  rectY = lcdHeight / 2 - RECT_SIZE / 2;


  /* TODO: Add input handling loop here */


  LCD_VRAMRestore();
  LCD_Refresh();
}
```

This code:

* Backs up the current VRAM content
* Gets the VRAM address and screen dimensions
* Centers the rectangle on the screen

## Step 6: Implement Input Handling

[Section titled “Step 6: Implement Input Handling”](#step-6-implement-input-handling)

This loop will:

* Draws the current state
* Waits for input events
* Handles touch events by moving the rectangle to the touch position
* Handles key events by moving the rectangle with arrow keys
* Exits when the CLEAR key is pressed
* Keeps the rectangle within screen boundaries

### Input Events

[Section titled “Input Events”](#input-events)

The app uses `GetInput()` to wait for events:

* `EVENT_TOUCH`: Touch screen events
* `EVENT_KEY`: Keyboard events

### Touch Handling

[Section titled “Touch Handling”](#touch-handling)

When the user touches the screen:

* `TOUCH_DOWN`: Initial touch
* `TOUCH_HOLD_DRAG`: Continued touch with movement

### Key Handling

[Section titled “Key Handling”](#key-handling)

The app responds to these keys:

* `KEYCODE_UP`: Move rectangle up
* `KEYCODE_DOWN`: Move rectangle down
* `KEYCODE_LEFT`: Move rectangle left
* `KEYCODE_RIGHT`: Move rectangle right
* `KEYCODE_POWER_CLEAR`: Exit the app

### Code

[Section titled “Code”](#code)

Add the main input handling loop:

```c++
  struct InputEvent event;
  bool running = true;


  while (running) {
    draw();


    GetInput(&event, 0xFFFFFFFF, 0x10);


    switch (event.type) {
    case EVENT_TOUCH:
      if (event.data.touch_single.direction == TOUCH_DOWN ||
          event.data.touch_single.direction == TOUCH_HOLD_DRAG) {
        rectX = event.data.touch_single.p1_x;
        rectY = event.data.touch_single.p1_y;
      }
      break;


    case EVENT_KEY:
      switch (event.data.key.keyCode) {
        case KEYCODE_UP:
          rectY -= MOVE_STEP;
          break;
        case KEYCODE_RIGHT:
          rectX += MOVE_STEP;
          break;
        case KEYCODE_DOWN:
          rectY += MOVE_STEP;
          break;
        case KEYCODE_LEFT:
          rectX -= MOVE_STEP;
          break;
        case KEYCODE_POWER_CLEAR:
          running = false;
          break;
      }
      break;
    }


    // Ensure the rectangle stays within the screen boundaries
    if (rectX < 0)
      rectX = 0;
    if (rectY < 0)
      rectY = 0;
    if (rectX + RECT_SIZE > lcdWidth)
      rectX = lcdWidth - RECT_SIZE;
    if (rectY + RECT_SIZE > lcdHeight)
      rectY = lcdHeight - RECT_SIZE;
  }
```

## Complete Example Code

[Section titled “Complete Example Code”](#complete-example-code)

Here’s the complete code for your TouchRectangle app:

```c++
#include <appdef.hpp>
#include <sdk/calc/calc.hpp>
#include <sdk/os/debug.hpp>
#include <sdk/os/input.hpp>
#include <sdk/os/lcd.hpp>


APP_NAME("TouchRectangle")
APP_DESCRIPTION("Move a rectangle based on touch and key input.")
APP_AUTHOR("Your Name")
APP_VERSION("1.0.0")


#define COLOR_BACKGROUND RGB_TO_RGB565(0, 0, 0)
#define COLOR_RECTANGLE RGB_TO_RGB565(0x1F, 0, 0)


#define RECT_SIZE 20
#define MOVE_STEP 5


extern uint16_t *vram;
int lcdWidth, lcdHeight;
int rectX, rectY;


void drawRectangle(int x, int y, uint16_t color) {
  for (int i = x; i < x + RECT_SIZE; ++i) {
    for (int j = y; j < y + RECT_SIZE; ++j) {
      if (i >= 0 && i < lcdWidth && j >= 0 && j < lcdHeight) {
        vram[i + (j + 24) * lcdWidth] = color;
      }
    }
  }
}


void draw() {
  LCD_ClearScreen();
  drawRectangle(rectX, rectY, COLOR_RECTANGLE);
  LCD_Refresh();
}


extern "C"
void main() {
  LCD_VRAMBackup();
  vram = LCD_GetVRAMAddress();
  LCD_GetSize(&lcdWidth, &lcdHeight);


  rectX = lcdWidth / 2 - RECT_SIZE / 2;
  rectY = lcdHeight / 2 - RECT_SIZE / 2;


  struct InputEvent event;


  bool running = true;
  while (running) {
    draw();


    GetInput(&event, 0xFFFFFFFF, 0x10);


    switch (event.type) {
    case EVENT_TOUCH:
      if (event.data.touch_single.direction == TOUCH_DOWN ||
          event.data.touch_single.direction == TOUCH_HOLD_DRAG) {
        rectX = event.data.touch_single.p1_x;
        rectY = event.data.touch_single.p1_y;
      }
      break;


    case EVENT_KEY:
      switch (event.data.key.keyCode) {
        case KEYCODE_UP:
          rectY -= MOVE_STEP;
          break;
        case KEYCODE_RIGHT:
          rectX += MOVE_STEP;
          break;
        case KEYCODE_DOWN:
          rectY += MOVE_STEP;
          break;
        case KEYCODE_LEFT:
          rectX -= MOVE_STEP;
          break;
        case KEYCODE_POWER_CLEAR:
          running = false;
          break;
      }
      break;
    }


    // Ensure the rectangle stays within the screen boundaries
    if (rectX < 0)
      rectX = 0;
    if (rectY < 0)
      rectY = 0;
    if (rectX + RECT_SIZE > lcdWidth)
      rectX = lcdWidth - RECT_SIZE;
    if (rectY + RECT_SIZE > lcdHeight)
      rectY = lcdHeight - RECT_SIZE;
  }


  LCD_VRAMRestore();
  LCD_Refresh();
}
```

# FAQ

> Frequently asked questions about ClassPad development, Hollyhock and gint.

Welcome to the **frequently asked questions** page! Here you’ll find simple answers to the questions that come up the most in our community — about Hollyhock, programming the calculator, and what’s actually going on inside that ClassPad of yours. If you’re brand new, this is a great place to start.

## What is Hollyhock?

[Section titled “What is Hollyhock?”](#what-is-hollyhock)

Hollyhock (HHK) is a **community-made modification** (a custom firmware add-on) for the Casio ClassPad II fx-CP400. Once installed, it lets your calculator run **custom programs** made by the community — games, tools, Python, and much more. There are two generations today: **V2** (the classic version) and **V3** (the current one). Hollyhock is built by the community, so everyone plays a part in making it better.

## What’s the difference between V2 and V3?

[Section titled “What’s the difference between V2 and V3?”](#whats-the-difference-between-v2-and-v3)

Back in the early V2 days (over 6 years ago), there was no shared compiler — everyone built their own local toolchain with custom patches, and V2 programs were **simple programs compiled for one fixed memory address**, a bit like burned ROM. That made programs very hard to build and port. **V3 fixes this**: programs are now real, standard **ELF files**, and the loader is **dynamic and flexible**, so it can support multiple OS versions — including future ones. Almost every V2 app has already been ported to V3, so V3 is the recommended version today.

## What is a .hh3 file?

[Section titled “What is a .hh3 file?”](#what-is-a-hh3-file)

A `.hh3` file is a **small ELF executable** : the standard executable format used on Linux. If you’re more familiar with Windows, think of it like a `.exe` file, but for your calculator. When you compile your C/C++ code, the compiler produces a `.hh3` file, and the Hollyhock launcher (“**YAL**”) loads it and runs your program.

## Can I still use V2?

[Section titled “Can I still use V2?”](#can-i-still-use-v2)

Yes! Switching between V2 and V3 is just a matter of swapping the `run.bin` file at the root of your calculator (V2 apps still work). That said, **V3 is recommended** as it is actively developed, more flexible, and nearly everything has been ported to it.

## Is my calculator backwards compatible between versions?

[Section titled “Is my calculator backwards compatible between versions?”](#is-my-calculator-backwards-compatible-between-versions)

Mostly, but **don’t expect perfect forward compatibility**. Apps made for one setup generally keep working, but there’s no guarantee that something built today will work on a future OS or firmware version without an update. When in doubt, check the [app store](https://classpaddev.github.io/store/) for the latest version of a program.

## How do I update back to the official OS?

[Section titled “How do I update back to the official OS?”](#how-do-i-update-back-to-the-official-os)

Before exams, we recommend restoring the official Casio OS so your calculator is not modified. Download the official updater from [TI-Planet’s archive](https://tiplanet.org/forum/archives_voir.php?id=5032905) [Mac Version](https://tiplanet.org/forum/archives_voir.php?id=5032910), then put the calculator in normal OS update mode.

On the calculator:

1. Connect the ClassPad to your computer with a standard USB cable.
2. When the USB menu appears, press `Clear` or choose `5: Cancel`.
3. Open the `Communication` app.
4. Open the top menu `Link`.
5. Choose `OS Update`, then press `OK`.
6. Leave the calculator alone until the update is complete. The screen will go blank, then the calculator will ask for touch screen alignment and initial setup again.

On the computer, wait 10 to 20 seconds for the USB drivers to install if needed, then click `OK` in the updater to start the official update. The update takes several minutes. Do not unplug the calculator while it is running.

## I’m new to programming : where should I start?

[Section titled “I’m new to programming : where should I start?”](#im-new-to-programming--where-should-i-start)

The community recommendation is to **start with Python**, using the calculator’s Python support. It’s forgiving, interactive, and you’ll learn how the calculator works along the way. Once you’re comfortable, moving to **C/C++** is natural as most of what you learned in Python still applies. A great entry point is the [Python app](https://classpaddev.github.io/store/p/python) and the [Python section of this wiki](/wiki/python/introduction/).

## What are the ways to make native programs?

[Section titled “What are the ways to make native programs?”](#what-are-the-ways-to-make-native-programs)

There are basically **two ways** to create native programs, and both produce `.hh3` files that look identical to the user:

1. **The Hollyhock native SDK** — it tries to **play as nicely as possible with the Casio OS**, so your hello world just prints on the screen as expected. This is the friendlier route.
2. **The gint kernel** — a custom kernel that **talks directly to the hardware**, ignoring most of the Casio OS. It’s the way to go if you want full control and performance: fast drawing, direct access to the LCD controller, USB, and so on. Most games are made with gint. See the [gint getting started guide](/wiki/gint/getting-started/introduction/).

It’s mostly a matter of which **template** you start from — the template guides your code quite a lot.

## Which compiler does the calculator use?

[Section titled “Which compiler does the calculator use?”](#which-compiler-does-the-calculator-use)

The Hollyhock native SDK uses a **recent GCC** toolchain that even supports modern C++, which is quite impressive for an embedded toolchain. The **gint** toolchain uses a **slightly older GCC with custom patches**. That’s also why we all prefer to use the same compiler — shared toolchains make troubleshooting *much* easier, and the two toolchains are **not interchangeable**.

## What CPU is inside the ClassPad?

[Section titled “What CPU is inside the ClassPad?”](#what-cpu-is-inside-the-classpad)

The fx-CP400 is powered by a **Hitachi (now Renesas) SuperH SH4A-DSP** — the same CPU family that powered the **Sega Dreamcast**, so we share a passion with the Dreamcast homebrew scene. The SuperH is a simple, well-designed Japanese architecture (you could call it the “grandma of ARM”). Because it’s an **SoC** (a single chip doing CPU, audio DSP, battery measurement and more) with almost no modern features, it’s actually a **wonderful chip to learn CPU basics** hands-on — things other platforms make deliberately hard to touch.

## Does it have an FPU?

[Section titled “Does it have an FPU?”](#does-it-have-an-fpu)

No — unlike the Dreamcast’s SH4, **the CP400’s CPU has no floating-point unit (FPU)**, the small extra circuit that computes decimal numbers like 3.14 very fast in hardware. Floating-point math is **emulated in software**, which is slower. Fun fact: in the 90s most CPUs had no FPU either — it’s the modern ones that are the exception! This limitation is exactly why the DSP and audio side of the chip is such an interesting thing to explore.

## How much RAM does it have?

[Section titled “How much RAM does it have?”](#how-much-ram-does-it-have)

The ClassPad has **around 16 MB of RAM** — an enormous amount for a calculator — but it’s split into **several regions** with different personalities: a small but **very fast** RAM intended for the DSP (audio), and larger but **slower** RAM for general use. There’s also **no MMU** (see the next question), so no virtual memory. Exploring the address space and learning which region is good for what is a fun part of ClassPad hacking.

## Why can’t programs load anywhere in memory like on a PC?

[Section titled “Why can’t programs load anywhere in memory like on a PC?”](#why-cant-programs-load-anywhere-in-memory-like-on-a-pc)

Because the ClassPad has **no MMU and no dynamic linker**. On a modern system like Linux, the dynamic linker loads programs and libraries at whatever position is free and fixes everything on the fly; the MMU also gives each program its own “virtual” memory so it believes it’s alone. On the ClassPad, code is **compiled for fixed load addresses** — if you load it somewhere else, all the addresses inside are wrong. The classic workaround is an **interpreter**: something like Python is essentially the “stub” you described — it reads bytecode from anywhere and executes it, just more slowly than native code.

## How does the screen work?

[Section titled “How does the screen work?”](#how-does-the-screen-work)

Two ways! You can either **write pixels into a buffer** — a large region of memory that gets mirrored to the screen — or **talk directly to the LCD controller** by sending commands to a memory address. The panel is **partially MIPI**, so a few basic commands (put pixel, refresh…) exist at the hardware level. Drawing directly to the LCD controller is the fastest route, and it’s one of the things gint makes easy.

## How fast is the CPU? Can I overclock it?

[Section titled “How fast is the CPU? Can I overclock it?”](#how-fast-is-the-cpu-can-i-overclock-it)

The CPU runs at around **100 MHz** and can be overclocked — tools like **CPtune** exist for that. In practice, keep it modest: the touchscreen stops responding when input polling goes above roughly **50 MHz** (it’s related to the I2C bus used by the touch controller), and memory limits (CL3 vs CL2 timings) also come into play. Don’t expect magic either — overclocking mostly makes the UI feel snappier, not necessarily your calculations.

## Can I compile on Linux?

[Section titled “Can I compile on Linux?”](#can-i-compile-on-linux)

**Yes, absolutely!** Both toolchains ship as **Docker images**, so you don’t need Windows at all:

* **Hollyhock native SDK**: `ghcr.io/classpaddev/hollyhock-3`
* **gint**: `ghcr.io/therainbowphoenix/gint-docker`

And if you want a **zero-setup** option, the templates work in **GitHub Codespaces** — you get a ready-to-code environment in your browser without installing anything.

## Is there a compiler that runs on the calculator itself?

[Section titled “Is there a compiler that runs on the calculator itself?”](#is-there-a-compiler-that-runs-on-the-calculator-itself)

Nothing concrete yet. The flash is small and **C compilers are hungry**, which makes self-hosting very difficult — though there have been projects trying to bring **TCC** (a tiny C compiler) to the calculator. For now, you’ll compile on your computer (or in Codespaces) and copy the `.hh3` file over.

## Where can I get help?

[Section titled “Where can I get help?”](#where-can-i-get-help)

The best place is our **Discord community**: [discord.gg/knpcNJTzpd](https://discord.gg/knpcNJTzpd). Hollyhock and the whole ClassPad development scene are community projects — the people writing the firmware, the SDKs and this wiki hang out there, and questions from beginners are always welcome. No question is too basic; we’ve all been there.

Still stuck?

If your question isn’t answered here, come **[join our Discord](https://discord.gg/knpcNJTzpd)** and ask! The community is friendly, and someone has almost certainly hit the same problem before. And hey — the calculator will make you much, much better at computers.

# Building your app

> Learn the process of building your Classpad app from the SDK.

If your devev is ready to be used, you shall be able to run the `make` command from the command line.

Building your Classpad app involves using the `make` command, a powerful tool for automating the compilation process. When you run `make bin`, it compiles your source code into a binary file. Similarly, `make hhk` generates an elf file for HollyHock2 but thoses are not recommended anymore.

## On the codespace / remote VSCode

[Section titled “On the codespace / remote VSCode”](#on-the-codespace--remote-vscode)

From the “**Explorer**” (*Ctrl + Shift + E*) panel at the top left, right click on the “main.cpp” file and choose “**Open in integrated terminal**”

![Right click on the "main.cpp" and open in terminal](/wiki/img/tutorials/main-open-in-term.png)

Inside the terminal, enter the following text : `make bin`

You should now see a file on the tree view ending with “**.bin**” (maybe *app\_template.bin*). Right click on it and choose “**Download…**”

Now, **plug your calculator** and put this file on the **root folder of the calculator** (not the *Autoimport*, the very **root folder that opens**).

Finally, unplug your calculator and on the *menu → System → Hollyhock-2 Launcher* and you should see your app on the list.

Not seeing your app ?

The app should be present on the **root of the calculator**, not into a subfolder. Also, there’s **sometime error** while copying the file. If so **try again one more time** just to be sure.

# Introduction

> Hollyhock2 aims to simplify, streamline, and optimize Classpad development, prioritizing an intuitive and high-performance experience for developers.

HollyHock2 operates as a modification (mod) for Classpad calculators, utilizing a **custom ROM** for enhanced functionality to make your calculator do even more **awesome things**. To make HHK work, you gotta **install it on your calculator**. If you haven’t done this yet, we have a **simple guide** to help you out. *Below that point are instructions for **advanced users**. You may skip them if you have successfuly setup the codespace.*

## Using the pre-built compiler

[Section titled “Using the pre-built compiler”](#using-the-pre-built-compiler)

Tip

The pre-built is tailored for **Windows** users only – *for now*.

To use the pre-built compiler for HollyHock2, follow these simple steps:

1. **Download the Files:** Go to [SH4-cross-mingw Releases](https://github.com/TheRainbowPhoenix/SH4-cross-mingw/releases) and download three files:

   * `build-all.zip`: Contains SH4 gcc for Windows and some helpers.
   * `tests.zip`: Includes test projects, build scripts, and make.
   * `hollyhock-2.zip`: The compiled SDK with the source.

2. **Create a Folder:** Create a new folder on your computer and name it, for example, “hhk”.

3. **Extract Files:**

   * Extract the contents of `build-all.zip`. The “out” folder should be extracted to the root of your “hhk” folder.
   * Extract the contents of `hollyhock-2.zip` to the root of the “hhk” folder.
   * Extract the contents of `tests.zip` to the “hhk” folder.

4. **Prepare for Build:** Navigate to the `tests/CPAppTemplate-main` folder and remove the `.hhk` and `.bin` files.

5. **Open CMD:** Open a Command Prompt (CMD) at the path of `tests/CPAppTemplate-main`:

   * Navigate to the folder’s address bar, type “cmd”, and press Enter.

6. **Build the App:** In the Command Prompt, type and execute the command: `build.bat`. This will build the app `hhk` and `bin`.

Your development environment is now set up, and you can start exploring and building with HollyHock2.

# Memory peek

> Read raw memory with exception guards

This advanced example reads raw memory and displays it as hexadecimal bytes. It is inspired by the memory browser in `Lephenixnoir/gintctl` on the Planet Casio git forge.

Some addresses cannot be read. The example installs a temporary exception handler so a bad read can be reported instead of crashing immediately.

## What it shows

[Section titled “What it shows”](#what-it-shows)

* Reading memory through a raw pointer
* Catching TLB miss and CPU read errors
* Skipping a faulting instruction with `gint_exc_skip()`
* Moving through memory with `UP` and `DOWN`

## Full source

[Section titled “Full source”](#full-source)

```c
#define FXCP
#include <stdint.h>
#include <stdbool.h>
#include <stdio.h>
#include <gint/display.h>
#include <gint/keyboard.h>
#include <gint/exc.h>


static uint32_t exception = 0;


static int catch_memory_exception(uint32_t code)
{
    if(code == 0x040 || code == 0x0e0) {
        exception = code;
        gint_exc_skip(1);
        return 0;
    }


    return 1;
}


static bool read_byte(uint8_t const *address, uint8_t *value)
{
    exception = 0;
    gint_exc_catch(catch_memory_exception);


    __asm__ volatile("mov.b @%1, %0" : "=r"(*value) : "r"(address));


    gint_exc_catch(NULL);
    return exception == 0;
}


static void draw_line(int y, uint32_t address)
{
    char bytes[32] = { 0 };
    char ascii[9] = { 0 };


    for(int i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
        uint8_t value = 0;


        if(!read_byte((void *)(address + i), &value)) {
            dprint(8, y, C_BLACK, "%08X: unreadable", address);
            return;
        }


        sprintf(bytes + 3 * i, "%02X ", value);
        ascii[i] = (value >= 0x20 && value < 0x7f) ? value : '.';
    }


    dprint(8, y, C_BLACK, "%08X: %s %s", address, bytes, ascii);
}


int main(void)
{
    uint32_t base = 0x88000000;


    while(1) {
        dclear(C_WHITE);
        dtext(8, 8, C_BLACK, "Memory peek");
        dtext(8, 28, C_BLACK, "UP/DOWN: move  EXIT: leave");


        for(int i = 0; i < 18; i++) {
            draw_line(70 + 20 * i, base + 8 * i);
        }


        dupdate();


        int key = getkey().key;
        if(key == KEY_EXIT) {
            return 1;
        }
        if(key == KEY_UP) {
            base -= 8 * 18;
        }
        if(key == KEY_DOWN) {
            base += 8 * 18;
        }
    }
}
```

## Notes

[Section titled “Notes”](#notes)

This is a debugging technique. Prefer normal pointers, buffers and file APIs when writing apps.

The exception handler is temporary: It is installed only around the risky memory read, then removed immediately after.

# Register browser

> Read hardware registers directly with gint

This advanced example reads a few hardware registers and prints their values. It is inspired by the register browser in `Lephenixnoir/gintctl` on the Planet Casio git forge.

Direct register access is useful when debugging drivers, clocks, interrupts, and low-level hardware state. It is also easy to misuse, so this example only reads registers.

## What it shows

[Section titled “What it shows”](#what-it-shows)

* Including `gint/mpu/*` headers
* Reading interrupt, power and clock registers
* Reading the CPU cache control register with a volatile pointer
* Displaying raw hexadecimal values

## Full source

[Section titled “Full source”](#full-source)

```c
#define FXCP
#include <stdint.h>
#include <gint/display.h>
#include <gint/keyboard.h>
#include <gint/mpu/intc.h>
#include <gint/mpu/power.h>
#include <gint/mpu/cpg.h>


int main(void)
{
    while(1) {
        dclear(C_WHITE);


        dtext(8, 8, C_BLACK, "Register browser");
        dtext(8, 28, C_BLACK, "Read-only hardware state");
        dtext(8, 48, C_BLACK, "Press EXIT to leave");


        dprint(8, 90, C_BLACK, "IPRA: %04x", SH7305_INTC._->IPRA.word);
        dprint(8, 110, C_BLACK, "IPRB: %04x", SH7305_INTC._->IPRB.word);
        dprint(8, 130, C_BLACK, "IPRC: %04x", SH7305_INTC._->IPRC.word);
        dprint(8, 150, C_BLACK, "IPRD: %04x", SH7305_INTC._->IPRD.word);


        dprint(8, 190, C_BLACK, "MSTPCR0: %08X", SH7305_POWER.MSTPCR0.lword);
        dprint(8, 210, C_BLACK, "MSTPCR2: %08X", SH7305_POWER.MSTPCR2.lword);


        dprint(8, 250, C_BLACK, "FSICLKCR: %08X", SH7305_CPG.FSICLKCR.lword);
        dprint(8, 270, C_BLACK, "SPUCLKCR: %08X", SH7305_CPG.SPUCLKCR.lword);


        volatile uint32_t *ccr = (void *)0xff00001c;
        dprint(8, 310, C_BLACK, "CCR: %08X", *ccr);


        dupdate();


        if(getkey().key == KEY_EXIT) {
            return 1;
        }
    }
}
```

## Notes

[Section titled “Notes”](#notes)

The `gint/mpu` headers expose mapped hardware registers as C structures. This is cleaner than manually hardcoding every address.

Only write to hardware registers when you know what the register does. A wrong write can freeze the calculator.

# Render timing

> Measure drawing and display update time with gint

This advanced example measures how long common rendering calls take. It is inspired by the render performance screen in `Lephenixnoir/gintctl` on the Planet Casio git forge.

The idea is simple: use `prof_make()`, `prof_enter()` and `prof_leave()` around a small operation, then print the elapsed time.

## What it shows

[Section titled “What it shows”](#what-it-shows)

* Measuring CPU time with `gint/prof.h`
* Comparing `dclear()`, `drect()` and `dupdate()`
* Keeping the display update measurement separate from drawing
* Using `KEY_EXE` to run the test again and `KEY_EXIT` to leave

## Full source

[Section titled “Full source”](#full-source)

```c
#define FXCP
#include <gint/display.h>
#include <gint/keyboard.h>
#include <gint/prof.h>
#include <fxlibc/printf.h>


struct results {
    uint32_t clear;
    uint32_t rect_small;
    uint32_t rect_full;
    uint32_t update;
};


static uint32_t measure(void (*function)(void))
{
    prof_t prof = prof_make();


    prof_enter(prof);
    function();
    prof_leave(prof);


    return prof_time(prof);
}


static void test_clear(void)
{
    dclear(C_WHITE);
}


static void test_rect_small(void)
{
    drect(0, 0, 31, 31, C_RGB(20, 20, 20));
}


static void test_rect_full(void)
{
    drect(0, 0, DWIDTH - 1, DHEIGHT - 1, C_RGB(20, 20, 20));
}


static void run_tests(struct results *r)
{
    r->clear = measure(test_clear);
    r->rect_small = measure(test_rect_small);
    r->rect_full = measure(test_rect_full);


    dclear(C_WHITE);
    dtext(8, 8, C_BLACK, "Measuring dupdate...");


    prof_t prof = prof_make();
    prof_enter(prof);
    dupdate();
    prof_leave(prof);
    r->update = prof_time(prof);
}


static void draw_results(struct results const *r)
{
    dclear(C_WHITE);
    dtext(8, 8, C_BLACK, "Render timing");
    dtext(8, 28, C_BLACK, "EXE: run  EXIT: leave");


    dprint(8, 70, C_BLACK, "dclear:       %.3D ms", r->clear);
    dprint(8, 90, C_BLACK, "drect 32x32:  %.3D ms", r->rect_small);
    dprint(8, 110, C_BLACK, "drect screen: %.3D ms", r->rect_full);
    dprint(8, 130, C_BLACK, "dupdate:      %.3D ms", r->update);


    dupdate();
}


int main(void)
{
    struct results r = { 0 };


    prof_init();
    __printf_enable_fixed();
    run_tests(&r);


    while(1) {
        draw_results(&r);


        int key = getkey().key;
        if(key == KEY_EXIT) {
            return 1;
        }
        if(key == KEY_EXE) {
            run_tests(&r);
        }
    }
}
```

## Notes

[Section titled “Notes”](#notes)

`prof_time()` returns a fixed-point millisecond value. The `%.3D` format prints it with three decimals after `__printf_enable_fixed()` is called.

`dupdate()` is measured separately because it sends VRAM to the screen. On ClassPad this cost matters a lot for animation-heavy programs.

# Introduction

> gint, the alternative unikernel for ClassPad development

gint (pronounced “guin”) is an add-in unikernel for Casio calculators. It was created by Lephenixnoir (Lephe), ported to the ClassPad by Lephe for Hollyhock-2, then by QBoss for Hollyhock-3, with the contribution of community members. What does “unikernel” mean for you? A gint program takes control of the calculator’s hardware from the Casio OS and manages it with its own drivers. Your app talks directly to the hardware instead of asking the Casio system to do things for you.

On ClassPad, nothing changes about how you run the app: a gint app is still a regular `.hh3` file loaded by the Hollyhock-3 launcher (YAL). The difference happens right after. Instead of handing control to your Casio OS code, the launcher hands control to the gint kernel, and from that moment your app is the boss of the machine.

There are two ways to build native add-ins on ClassPad: gint and the [Hollyhock-3 SDK](/wiki/hh3/getting-started/introduction/). Both produce the same `.hh3` files, so for the user they look identical. We recommend gint for games and anything that needs performance, and the Hollyhock SDK for regular programs. If you learned [Python](/wiki/python/introduction/) on the calculator first, gint will feel familiar since the Python support is built on it. If you want newer C++ and experimental features, the Hollyhock SDK is the better choice.

One thing to keep in mind: gint programs on the ClassPad are largely limited in size. The whole program has to fit in a fixed load region of about 330 KiB (337,920 bytes, an area the calculator uses as a VRAM backup) defined by the gint linker script.

## What gint offers on ClassPad

[Section titled “What gint offers on ClassPad”](#what-gint-offers-on-classpad)

The ClassPad port (gint 2.11.0) already gives you a lot of powerful hardware access:

* An own LCD driver for the fx-CP400 screen (Renesas R61523, 320x528 portrait RGB565), with efficient rendering functions (`dclear`, `dtext`, image rendering, and more).
* KEYSC keyboard support plus an I2C touchscreen driver, so you get real touch events with x/y coordinates.
* Hardware timers with sub-millisecond resolution. Great for games and animation.
* Interrupt management, user-extendable and efficient.
* A memory allocator (kmalloc).
* Fugue filesystem access, so you can read and write the files the calculator already uses.

In general, better performance is the main reason games are built with gint. When your code owns the hardware, every cycle counts.

## Current limitations on ClassPad (for now)

[Section titled “Current limitations on ClassPad (for now)”](#current-limitations-on-classpad-for-now)

We want to be honest with you: the ClassPad port is still young, and a few things are not available yet:

* Serial communication is not available yet. There is no serial/UART driver on the CP400 port.
* DMA is not working yet, so display updates are CPU-driven for now.
* USB is not functional yet on the ClassPad port.
* No overclock control from gint yet.
* A gint app does not return to the Casio menu when it exits. The launcher regains control, and there is no way back into the OS until it is restarted.

These are all port progress items, not permanent limitations. The underlying hardware (and in many cases the upstream gint code) already supports them. Stay tuned!

## Templates to get you started

[Section titled “Templates to get you started”](#templates-to-get-you-started)

[⛩️ Gint Template ](https://github.com/TheRainbowPhoenix/gint-template)Recommended starting point for a simple gint app on ClassPad

[📱 Gint + JustUI Template ](https://github.com/TheRainbowPhoenix/USB_test)Gint template in C with JustUI, touchscreen-ready. For a bare-bones alternative, see the gint-template repository

You cannot mix gint headers with the native SDK. They are two independent worlds, each with its own compiler and libraries. The good news: each template comes with its own Docker image / devcontainer, so there is nothing to configure manually. Open the template and start coding!
