# Understanding how gint works

> What the fx-CP400 hardware and the gint kernel do when your program runs

This page is a technical tour of the machine and the kernel. You do not need it to write a first program, but it explains what actually happens between `fxsdk build-cp` and your `main()`, and what the hardware can and cannot do for you while your code runs. Everything here is based on the ClassPad port of gint (target fxCP, version 2.11.0); where the port differs from the fx-9860G and fx-CG 50 versions, the ClassPad behavior is the one described.

## The machine

[Section titled “The machine”](#the-machine)

The ClassPad II (fx-CP400) is built around a Renesas [SH7305](/wiki/hardware/cpu/73050/), a SuperH SH4A core running at about 118 MHz. Three properties of this chip shape everything you do in a gint program.

First, there is no usable [FPU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Floating-point_unit). The toolchain targets the no-FPU variant of the SH4A and gint does not enable the coprocessor, so every `float` and `double` operation is a call into software floating-point code from OpenLibm. Fixed-point arithmetic with plain integers is almost always faster.

Second, there is no [MMU](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memory_management_unit) in play. Hardware detection in the port records that there is no userspace and no MMU in use, and `gint[HWURAM]` is 0. The 16 MiB of RAM form one flat address space. Pointers are physical addresses. There is no memory protection, so a stray pointer does not fault, it corrupts whatever it touches, including the kernel and the launcher. Most of RAM is visible around `0x8c000000`, which is the cached view of memory.

Third, memory is not uniform. The CPU has a small cache over main RAM, and there are on-chip memory areas that sit outside the cache path and are faster than main RAM:

| Region             | Address    | Size   | Use                                |
| ------------------ | ---------- | ------ | ---------------------------------- |
| Main RAM           | 0x8c000000 | 16 MiB | Everything: code, data, heap, VRAM |
| On-chip X/Y memory | 0xe500e000 | 16 KiB | Fast storage, `xyram` section      |
| On-chip IL memory  | 0xe5200000 | 4 KiB  | Fast storage, `ilram` section      |

Main RAM itself varies: access through the cache is fast, uncached access (addresses seen at `0xa0000000` instead of `0x8c000000`) is slow. The LCD hangs on a 16-bit external bus.

The screen is a Renesas R61523 in a 320x528 portrait layout, 16 bits per pixel in RGB565. The panel is not memory-mapped. You push pixels to it through a register window at `0xb4000000`, one write per pixel, with a GPIO bit selecting command or data. See the driver in [r61523.c](https://github.com/ClasspadDev/gint/blob/dev/src/r61523/r61523.c).

Because there is no MMU and no protection, the usual discipline matters more than on a desktop. Peripheral registers must be accessed through `volatile` pointers. Writes to external-bus devices need `synco()` barriers so the store actually reaches the wire before the next one. And any wild write is a real crash, not an exception with a nice stack trace.

One last piece of the machine: the CPU can stop. `sleep()` from `<gint/cpu.h>` executes the SuperH sleep instruction and halts the core until the next interrupt. gint uses it internally in `waitevent()` and you should use it in idle loops too. It saves battery and it is free.

For a sense of what this chip can do in good hands, here is a talk about how Doom was made to run on a calculator, and what it took to get there.

[How Doom Pushed a Calculator Beyond Its Limits](https://www.youtube.com/embed/LimTt0nn0IU)

## From source to .hh3

[Section titled “From source to .hh3”](#from-source-to-hh3)

`fxsdk build-cp` is a wrapper. It sets the platform to fxCP, points CMake at the cross-compilation toolchain file, and runs the build. Your project’s `CMakeLists.txt` does the rest:

```cmake
include(GenerateHH3)
find_package(Gint 2.9 REQUIRED)
find_package(JustUI 1.0 REQUIRED)


target_link_libraries(myaddin Gint::Gint JustUI::JustUI)


if("${FXSDK_PLATFORM_LONG}" STREQUAL fxCP)
  generate_hh3(TARGET myaddin OUTPUT "MyAddin.hh3")
endif()
```

CMake compiles your sources with `sh-elf-gcc`, a big-endian SuperH compiler with no FPU. Assets listed with `fxconv_declare_assets()` are converted to C data at build time. The link step uses the gint-provided script [fxcp\_hh3.ld.c](https://github.com/ClasspadDev/gint/blob/dev/fxcp_hh3.ld.c), which places every section at fixed addresses in RAM. The result is a static ELF: no dynamic linking, no relocation at load time, everything resolved at link time.

`generate_hh3` strips the ELF and the stripped file is your `.hh3`. The ELF also carries metadata notes built by the `HHK_NAME`, `HHK_DESCRIPTION`, `HHK_AUTHOR` and `HHK_VERSION` macros from `<gint/config.h>`. These land in a `.note.hollyhock` section and are what the launcher reads to show your app’s name and description.

### The toolchain

[Section titled “The toolchain”](#the-toolchain)

The pieces are built from source and installed into the compiler’s search path. In dependency order:

1. `sh-elf-binutils`: assembler, linker, binutils for SuperH.
2. `sh-elf-gcc`: the compiler. Needs binutils at build time, needs them again at install time.
3. `fxlibc`: the C standard library, compiled with the new compiler.
4. `gint` and `JustUI`: the kernel and the UI toolkit, which link against fxlibc and OpenLibm.

`fxsdk` itself is a Python program that glues it all together, and `sh-elf-gdb` is a separate, optional debugger. All of these ship with `giteapc.make` files, so GiteaPC can build and install them in the right order with one command per repository. The gint-docker image does exactly this; if you would rather not build the toolchain, use `ghcr.io/therainbowphoenix/gint-docker` as a devcontainer and skip the whole section.

If you install manually, use the dev branch of each repository. Lephe’s originals live on the Planete Casio forge, and Phoebe keeps mirrors of the toolchain repos (fxsdk, sh-elf-binutils, sh-elf-gcc, fxlibc and friends) on git.xania.fr. The default branches are often outdated relative to dev, and the ClassPad port in particular needs recent gint.

## Memory layout of a running app

[Section titled “Memory layout of a running app”](#memory-layout-of-a-running-app)

The linker script is the contract. It defines four RAM regions:

| Region  | Address                | Size         | Content                                  |
| ------- | ---------------------- | ------------ | ---------------------------------------- |
| `ram`   | 0x8c052800             | 337920 bytes | Your whole program                       |
| `eram`  | 0x8cff0000             | 61184 bytes  | Extra sections (`.hh3*`, `.eram*`)       |
| `vbr`   | 0x8cffef00             | 4352 bytes   | VBR and interrupt handler tables         |
| on-chip | 0xe500e000, 0xe5200000 | 20 KiB       | Fast scratch (`xyram`, `ilram` sections) |

The main region deserves attention. 337920 bytes is exactly 320x528x2, the size of a full framebuffer. It is the Casio OS’s VRAM backup area, memory that the OS keeps free because it uses it to save the screen. Hollyhock-3 itself is loaded at 0x8cfd0000, 128 KiB below the end of RAM, which is why the extra regions are squeezed in above it. Your code, your data, your BSS and everything else must fit in that one area. A single static array of `uint16_t[320*528]` would consume it entirely.

Inside the region, the script lays out, in order: the Hollyhock notes, `.text` (starting with the entry point, then constructors and destructors, then the exception and TLB handler stubs, then all code), the interrupt handler blocks, the driver table, `.rodata`, `.data`, `.bss`, and finally `.gint.bss` where gint puts its own large uninitialized buffers. Everything above the end of `.gint.bss` is yours but unused; since the region is a fixed-size window, unused space cannot be given back to anyone.

The eram region exists because some things cannot live in the main region. It holds sections named `.hh3*` and `.eram*`, which you only use deliberately. The on-chip regions are more interesting: sections named `.ilram` and `.xyram` are loaded into ILRAM and XYRAM by the launcher like any other segment, so you can place hot code or data there with a section attribute and get memory that is faster than main RAM. 20 KiB total is not much, so the usual use is a small function or a set of counters rather than buffers.

One special address sits below your program. The Casio OS keeps its own framebuffer at 0x8c000000, and gint uses that exact buffer as its VRAM, as you can see in [dvram.c](https://github.com/ClasspadDev/gint/blob/dev/src/render-cg/dvram.c). At boot, gint compresses the current screen content and keeps the compressed copy on the heap, so it can restore the previous display when the program exits. You never see this; just be aware that the 330 KiB below your program is not free either.

The stack is inherited from the launcher: YAL calls your entry point on its own stack and the kernel keeps it. Keep stack frames reasonable; there is no separate kernel stack for your program.

## Boot

[Section titled “Boot”](#boot)

Starting a gint app goes through three layers. The launcher, then the Hollyhock entry shim, then the kernel.

YAL scans storage memory for `.hh3` files, shows the list, and when you pick one it loads the ELF. The loader in YAL reads the program headers, copies each `PT_LOAD` segment’s file contents to its virtual address, zeroes the remainder up to `p_memsz` (this is how your BSS is wiped), then flushes the cache over every loaded byte so the CPU does not execute stale cache lines. It validates that the file is a static SuperH executable, builds `argv` with the file path, and calls the entry point with `argc`, `argv` and `environ`.

YAL also puts two variables in the environment: `HHK_SYMBOL_TABLE` and `HHK_SYMBOL_TABLE_LEN`, as hex strings. The table is a list of name and address pairs for Casio OS functions that Hollyhock-3 exposes. The first entry is a version string which is checked against the OS version in ROM, to catch symbol tables built for a different OS.

Your entry point is `_hhk3_entry`, defined in [hhk3\_start.c](https://github.com/ClasspadDev/gint/blob/dev/src/kernel/hhk3_start.c). It walks the symbol table and copies the address of each known symbol into a global variable. The list is short and practical: `Mem_Malloc` and `Mem_Free` for the OS heap, and the `File_*` family for filesystem access. It also installs a custom `realloc` built on those two. If the environment variables or the table are missing, it panics with a specific code (0x2020 and friends), which is what you see if you run a gint app outside Hollyhock-3. Then it calls `start()`.

`start()` in [start.c](https://github.com/ClasspadDev/gint/blob/dev/src/kernel/start.c) is the C runtime. On the ClassPad it is short because the loader already copied `.data` and zeroed `.bss`. It detects the hardware, then calls `kinit()` in [kernel.c](https://github.com/ClasspadDev/gint/blob/dev/src/kernel/kernel.c), which does the real installation:

1. Initialize kmalloc and its arenas.
2. Allocate the two world buffers (driver state snapshots for the OS world and the gint world) and the driver flags.
3. Initialize the VRAM, which includes backing up the current screen.
4. Call every driver constructor, in priority order.
5. Copy the exception, TLB and interrupt handler entry points into the VBR region and switch the VBR over.

From this point interrupts go to gint, not to Casio’s handlers. Control then passes to your constructors, and `main()` runs. The call is wrapped in `setjmp(gint_exitbuf)`: when your program calls `exit()` or returns from `main()`, control longjmps back, destructors run, and `kquit()` restores the drivers and the VBR to their saved state before returning the exit code to YAL.

If something goes wrong during this process or later, the CPU raises an exception and gint’s exception handler in [exch.c](https://github.com/ClasspadDev/gint/blob/dev/src/kernel/exch.c) catches it. The default handler draws a panic screen in the style of the Casio System ERROR, with the exception code, the faulting PC and the fault address, and stops there. `gint_panic()` triggers the same screen with a custom code, which is how the entry shim reports a missing symbol table. You can install your own handler with `gint_panic_set()` if you would rather die differently.

There is no return to the Casio OS. On fx-9860G and fx-CG 50, gint can pop the calculator’s main menu and come back. On the ClassPad that machinery does not exist: `gint_setrestart()` is a no-op and `gint_osmenu()` has no effect. When your `main()` returns, the program is over and the launcher gets control back.

Caution

There is no way back. Once `main()` returns, the gint application is finished and there is no Casio menu to resume it from. Structure your program around one main loop that runs as long as the user wants it to, not around exiting and restarting.

To summarize the whole path from the launcher to your code:

1. YAL lists the `.hh3` files, you pick one, the ELF is validated and its segments are copied to their fixed addresses, cache flushed.
2. YAL exports the OS symbol table in the environment and calls the entry point.
3. `hhk3_entry()` resolves `Mem_Malloc`, `Mem_Free` and the `File_*` functions from the table.
4. `start()` detects the hardware and `kinit()` installs kmalloc, the worlds, the drivers and the VBR.
5. Constructors run, then `main()`.

## Drivers and world switching

[Section titled “Drivers and world switching”](#drivers-and-world-switching)

A gint driver is a piece of code that owns one hardware module. Each driver declares a state buffer, a priority, and a set of lifecycle functions: power on and off, save and restore state, configure, and bind and unbind. The table in [drivers.h](https://github.com/ClasspadDev/gint/blob/dev/include/gint/drivers.h) explains the vocabulary: a device is powered if its clock is on, bound if a driver has exclusive access, and configured if it is set up for use.

The priorities fix the startup order, and the same order is reused for state snapshots:

| Priority | Driver   | Manages                        |
| -------- | -------- | ------------------------------ |
| 0        | cpu      | CPU registers, atomic sections |
| 1        | intc     | Interrupt controller           |
| 2        | mmu      | TLB (mostly inert here)        |
| 5        | cpg, dma | Clocks, DMA controller         |
| 13       | rtc, tmu | Real-time clock, timers        |
| 16       | usb      | USB controller                 |
| 22       | touch    | Touchscreen                    |
| 23       | keysc    | Keyboard                       |
| 26       | r61523   | LCD                            |

The interesting concept is the world. A world is a snapshot of every driver’s state. gint keeps two of them: one for the Casio OS environment as it was at boot, one for itself. `gint_world_switch()` in [world.c](https://github.com/ClasspadDev/gint/blob/dev/src/kernel/world.c) saves the gint world, restores the OS world, runs the function you pass (build one with `GINT_CALL()`), then switches back. This is the mechanism that makes gint a hypervisor of sorts: the OS never learns that someone else drove its hardware in the meantime.

On the ClassPad this mechanism is much less central than on the other calculators. gint talks to the filesystem through Hollyhock’s `File_*` functions directly, with no switch, and there is no OS menu to reach. You will rarely need `gint_world_switch()`. `gint_world_sync()` is still relevant to wait for asynchronous driver work to finish.

## Drawing

[Section titled “Drawing”](#drawing)

The drawing API is the `d*` family from `<gint/display.h>`: `dclear()`, `drect()`, `dline()`, `dcircle()`, `dpoly()`, `dtext()`, `dimage()`, and friends. All of them draw into the VRAM pointer `gint_vram`, a `uint16_t *` buffer of 320x528 pixels. Nothing reaches the panel until you call `dupdate()`.

Colors are 16-bit RGB565, big-endian, the format the controller consumes. Build them with `C_RGB(r, g, b)`, three channels of 5 bits, or use the named colors `C_WHITE`, `C_BLACK` and so on. `C_NONE` means transparent in functions that support it.

On the fx-CG 50, `dupdate()` hands the frame to the DMA controller and returns early, which is why that port can afford triple buffering. The ClassPad port has no working DMA path yet, so [dupdate()](https://github.com/ClasspadDev/gint/blob/dev/src/render-cg/dupdate.c) does the whole job on the CPU: it programs the R61523 window registers and writes all 337920 bytes through the 16-bit bus, one store at a time. This is a large, synchronous cost, and it is paid while your program is blocked.

The consequence for design is simple. Render a complete frame, call `dupdate()` once, then go do your computation, then render the next frame. Avoid pushing partial frames in a loop. Measure with `prof` if frame budget matters to you, and remember that the numbers from fx-CG 50 discussions do not transfer: different bus, different driver. Two smaller controls are available: `dwindow_set()` clips all rendering to a sub-rectangle, and `dupdate_set_hook()` registers a callback invoked after each update, meant for capturing frames to another medium.

Text goes through topti, gint’s font engine. gint ships a default font; `dfont()` installs another one, and fonts are produced from PNG or template files by fxconv at build time. Text rendering supports proportional and monospaced fonts, colors, and alignment through `dtext_opt()` and `dprint()` (printf-style).

Images use the `image_t` model from `<gint/image.h>`. Formats are RGB565, RGB565 with one transparent color, and 8-bit or 4-bit palette variants of both.

| Format             | Storage                              | Pixel size  |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------ | ----------- |
| `IMAGE_RGB565`     | Direct 16-bit color                  | 2 bytes     |
| `IMAGE_RGB565A`    | Direct 16-bit color, one transparent | 2 bytes     |
| `IMAGE_P8_RGB565A` | 8-bit palette index                  | 1 byte      |
| `IMAGE_P4_RGB565A` | 4-bit palette index                  | half a byte |

Indexed formats save memory and render faster at the cost of a palette, which makes P8 the usual choice for sprites. Rendering handles transparent and palette formats, and a set of transform functions (scaling, rotation, hflip) exists in the image library. fxconv converts your PNG assets into these formats during the build; the palette is extracted automatically, or provided explicitly if you need fixed indices.

## Input and time

[Section titled “Input and time”](#input-and-time)

The keyboard is a KEYSC matrix scanned by a hardware timer. gint runs the scan at 128 Hz by default, configurable from 64 Hz to 32768 Hz with `keysc_set_scan_frequency()`. Each tick produces the raw 12-byte matrix state, compares it with the previous one, and generates events.

The event model in `<gint/keyboard.h>` is a queue of `key_event_t`. Each event has a type (`KEYEV_DOWN`, `KEYEV_UP`, `KEYEV_HOLD` for repeats), a keycode, a timestamp in scan cycles, and modifier flags for SHIFT and ALPHA. You read the queue with `pollevent()` (non-blocking), `waitevent()` (blocking), or drain it with `clearevents()`. The alternative style is `getkey()`, a blocking call that handles modifiers, key repetition, and the MENU key for you, closer to the OS’s GetKey(). Event-driven code with `pollevent()` suits games; `getkey()` suits text input and menus. On the ClassPad, keep in mind that the MENU key brings up nothing: the OS menu path in `getkey()` targets the other models and ends in a no-op here.

The touchscreen plugs into the same queue. It is an I2C device; the driver reads raw samples from the controller over I2C and, on every keyboard scan tick, converts them with a calibration table into screen coordinates. Touch events have types `KEYEV_TOUCH_DOWN`, `KEYEV_TOUCH_DRAG` and `KEYEV_TOUCH_UP`, and carry `x` and `y` fields. The calibration data comes from `touch_calib_get()`, which can read the OS’s own calibration. One event per scan tick is the maximum rate, so touch input has the granularity of the 128 Hz scan, not of the I2C device.

One keyboard behavior is baked into the kernel and worth knowing before it surprises you: pressing SHIFT, 7, 3 and AC/ON together calls `abort()` and kills the add-in. This is the freeze escape hatch inherited from the other models.

Time comes from two places. The TMU timers are the precise ones: `timer_configure(TIMER_ANY, delay, callback)` gives you a periodic callback, with a resolution of about 250 ns on a TMU and about 30 us on the extra ETMU timers. The SH7305 has three TMUs and six ETMUs, and gint uses one ETMU for the keyboard scan, so plan for the count. Sub-millisecond delays are realistic. The RTC is coarser but absolute: `rtc_ticks()` returns 128 Hz ticks since midnight, and `rtc_get_time()` gives the calendar. Use a timer for frame pacing, the RTC for wall-clock time.

For measurement, `<gint/prof.h>` runs a TMU as a free-running counter. `prof_enter()` and `prof_leave()` bracket a region, and `prof_time()` converts the elapsed counts to microseconds. `prof_exec({ ... })` measures a one-shot block in a single expression.

## Memory allocation

[Section titled “Memory allocation”](#memory-allocation)

`malloc()` in a gint program goes through fxlibc’s hardware abstraction layer into `kmalloc()`, the allocator in [src/kmalloc/](https://github.com/ClasspadDev/gint/blob/dev/src/kmalloc/kmalloc.c). kmalloc manages several independent arenas; a plain `malloc()` searches the default arenas in turn.

On the ClassPad the picture is minimal. There is no static RAM arena like on the other models, since all of your static RAM is inside the load region already. The only default arena is the OS heap, which wraps `Mem_Malloc` and `Mem_Free` from the symbol table. So a heap allocation is a call into Hollyhock’s allocator, operating on the Casio OS’s own heap, which is outside your 330 KiB and typically much larger.

You can add arenas yourself with `kmalloc_init_arena()` and `kmalloc_add_arena()`. The classic use is to carve a block out of on-chip memory or out of memory you own, either for speed or to control fragmentation. `kmalloc_max()` grabs the largest block of an arena whole. Arenas managed by gint’s allocator also track statistics (live blocks, peak, total volume, failures) that you can read for debugging.

Two practical warnings. First, memory you allocate on the OS heap never frees back into your load region, so the split is rigid: static data shrinks your program, heap data does not. Second, the OS heap is shared with the OS and the launcher. Fragmentation there is real: prefer few, long-lived allocations over many small ones, free everything, and do not assume allocation order will keep the heap tidy. For a game, the usual pattern is to allocate all buffers once at startup and never call malloc after that.

## Files, USB and serial

[Section titled “Files, USB and serial”](#files-usb-and-serial)

The calculator’s storage uses the Fugue filesystem. gint’s POSIX layer (`open()`, `read()`, `write()`, `opendir()` and the rest, from `<gint/fs.h>` and the standard headers) is implemented on top of Fugue in [src/fs/fugue/](https://github.com/ClasspadDev/gint/blob/dev/src/fs/fugue/fugue.c). On the other platforms this layer has to drop back to the OS with a world switch before every BFile call. On the ClassPad it does not: the `File_*` functions resolved at boot are called directly, so file access is available at any time, including from inside interrupt callbacks if you are careful.

Paths are ordinary strings in the Fugue style, rooted at the flash volume. The 16-bit `FONTCHARACTER` encoding of the other models is gone; this is a plain `char *` interface, closer to POSIX, with its own errno-style error codes that the fugue layer maps to standard `errno` values. Fugue itself is slow, especially for writes; do not expect filesystem calls inside a frame loop. One implementation detail is worth knowing: Fugue cannot write data that sits in flash-mapped ROM, so `write()` on a constant buffer first copies it to a RAM block. Passing large read-only buffers to `write()` therefore costs an extra copy.

USB is a different story. gint has a full USB driver with a class framework and the fxlink bulk transfer class, but it is not working on the ClassPad port yet. The driver may be present in the binary, but do not build features on it. Serial support is in the same category: the header `<gint/serial.h>` exists, the implementation does not. Write code as if neither exists, and check the gint repository’s TODO for port status if you want to follow the work.

Caution

USB and serial are not functional on the ClassPad port. Do not call `usb_open()`, the fxlink functions, or the serial API; they will not do what you expect.

## How to think when you code for gint

[Section titled “How to think when you code for gint”](#how-to-think-when-you-code-for-gint)

Your program owns the machine. There is no scheduler, no other process, no preemption except interrupts you configured. Your `main()` loop is free to spin at full speed, and every microsecond it does not spend is wasted. This is the entire performance argument for gint.

A few habits that follow from the hardware:

* Think integer. Software floating point costs orders of magnitude more than integer math. Use fixed-point with shifts, or precompute tables.
* Keep static data small. Every global and every string literal sits in your 330 KiB load region, along with all the code. Large tables belong in flash-friendly read-only sections, and buffers in the heap.
* Respect the frame budget. Draw the frame, call `dupdate()` once, then compute. If you need to know where the time goes, `prof_exec()` gives you exact numbers.
* Allocate once. Collect all your buffers at startup, free them on exit, and keep the OS heap stable in between.
* Sleep when idle. If you are waiting on input or time, `sleep()` inside the wait loop; the CPU costs nothing while halted.
* Pair `cpu_atomic_start()` and `cpu_atomic_end()` around manipulation of shared state, and use `volatile` for anything an interrupt handler or a peripheral can change behind your back.
* Do not rely on exiting. There is no menu to return to and no save state; design the program to run until the user is done, then exit cleanly.

Where to look next:

* The gint repository’s TODO tracks the ClassPad port status: what works, what is in progress, what is not.
* gintctl is gint’s test and monitoring program; its sources show drivers, rendering and profiling used at full depth (currently targeted at the other models, but the patterns transfer).
* JustUI, the widget toolkit that pairs with gint, is worth reading before building any nontrivial interface; see the JustUI sources.
* The `include/gint/` headers are heavily documented and are the real API reference; start with `gint.h`, `display.h`, `keyboard.h` and `timer.h`.

# BFile

> BFile interface

Unofficial documentation

Community-written docs, valid for the ClassPad port only, possibly slightly outdated. They will be replaced by the official gint documentation once it is published.

BFile is the OS’s native interface to the filesystem. It has quite a bit of legacy, so it’s not very easy to use. Please note that BFile cannot be used from within gint, so do a gint\_world\_switch() (\<gint/gint.h>) to call BFile functions; otherwise the add-in is likely to crash.

There are two different filesystems:

* An older, in-house one made by CASIO and informally called CASIOWIN (which is the name of the OS itself), which is incomplete, hard to use, and very limiting, but also very fast.
* A newer one, designed by Kyoto Software Research and called Fugue, which is mostly complete and behaves as a regular filesystem, though very slow.

You can detect which one is used by querying gint\[HWFS] (\<gint/hardware.h>):

* HWFS\_FUGUE is the newer one; it is found in:

- The fx-CG series (in France: Prizm and Graph 90+E)
- The fx G-III series (in France: Graph 35+E II)

* HWFS\_CASIOWIN is the older one; it is found in all older black-and-white model that have a storage memory.

Wherever Fugue is used, gint supports the Unix file API (open, read, write, etc) and the C99 standard file API (fopen, fread, fwrite, etc), so there is no need to call into BFile directly (you should still do a world switch before using these functions).

You should only have to use BFile if you’re dealing with the CASIOWIN filesystem. With Fugue, not only are the Unix/C99 APIs easier to use, but the meanings of arguments and return values in BFile calls also change compared to the CASIOWIN filesystem, so there’s little to gain anyway.

If you’re here for the CASIOWIN filesystem, be aware of its limitations. In general reading files will work fine; expect no issues with that. Modifying files is where things get difficult. Keep the following in mind:

* Non-standard meanings of arguments and return values (eg. BFile\_Read() returns the number of readable bytes between the new position and EOF).
* Files must be created with a fixed size indicated in BFile\_Create() and are initialized with 0xff.
* A write to a file can only replace 1’s with 0’s, meaning in practice a file can only be written to once. (That’s why it’s created with 0xff.)
* All writes must be of even size; writing an odd number of bytes can mess up the file and confuse the filesystem.
* Only one level of folders is supported; attempting to create second-level subfolders results in weird recursive directories (don’t do that).

File paths in the OS use the non-standard FONTCHARACTER encoding, which is a 16-bit fixed-width encoding. Most users don’t care about special characters; in GCC, you can get a 16-bit literal string with the u"" prefix, eg. u”\\\fls0\data.bin” which is what you usually supply as the \[uint16\_t const \*path] argument.

All functions return nonnegative values on success. If no return value is described then a successful call returns 0. Unless specified otherwise, all functions can also return a negative error code as documented near the end of this header.

***

### `clock_get_speed`

[Section titled “clock\_get\_speed”](#clock_get_speed)

clock\_get\_speed(): Determine the current clock speed

This function compares the current hardware state with the settings for each speed level and returns the current one. If the hardware state does not correspond to any of Ftune’s settings, CLOCK\_SPEED\_UNKNOWN is returned.

```c
int clock_get_speed(void)
```

***

### `clock_set_speed`

[Section titled “clock\_set\_speed”](#clock_set_speed)

clock\_set\_speed(): Set the current clock speed

This function sets the clock speed to the desired level. This is “the overclock function”, although depending on the model or settings it is also the downclocking function.

The process of changing clock speeds is non-trivial, requires waiting for the DMA to finish its work and slightly affects running timers. You should avoid changing the clock speed constantly if not necessary. If this function detects that the desired clock speed is already in use, it returns without performing any change.

Currently the clock speed is not reset during a world switch nor when leaving the add-in.

```c
void clock_set_speed(int speed)
```

***

## Data structures

[Section titled “Data structures”](#data-structures)

The following enumerations define the clock speed settings supported by gint. These are always the settings from Ftune/Ptune, which are the most widely tested and gint treats as the standard.

```c
enum
{
  /* Combinations of hardware settings that are none of Ftune's levels */ CLOCK_SPEED_UNKNOWN = 0, /* Ftune's 5 default overclock levels. The main settings are listed below, though many more are involved. On SH3 fx-9860G-like: F1: CPU @ 29 MHz [Default speed] F2: CPU @ 58 MHz [Similar to G-III default] F3: CPU @ 88 MHz F4: CPU @ 118 MHz [Fastest CPU option] F5: CPU @ 118 MHz [Reduced memory wait times] On SH4 fx-9860G-like: F1: CPU @ 29 MHz, BFC @ 29 MHz [Default speed] F2: CPU @ 58 MHz, BFC @ 29 MHz [Similar to G-III default] F3: CPU @ 29 MHz, BFC @ 29 MHz [SH3 default] F4: CPU @ 118 MHz, BFC @ 59 MHz F5: CPU @ 236 MHz, BFC @ 118 MHz [Fastest option] On G-III / Graph 35+E II: F1: CPU @ 58 MHz, BFC @ 29 MHz [Default speed] F2: CPU @ 58 MHz, BFC @ 29 MHz [fx-CG 10/20 default] F3: CPU @ 29 MHz, BFC @ 29 MHz [SH3 default] F4: CPU @ 118 MHz, BFC @ 58 MHz F5: CPU @ 235 MHz, BFC @ 58 MHz [Fastest option] On fx-CG 10/20: F1: CPU @ 58 MHz, BFC @ 29 MHz [Default speed] F2: CPU @ 58 MHz, BFC @ 29 MHz [Improved memory speed] F3: CPU @ 118 MHz, BFC @ 58 MHz [Faster than F2] F4: CPU @ 118 MHz, BFC @ 118 MHz [Fastest bus option] F5: CPU @ 191 MHz, BFC @ 94 MHz [Fastest CPU option] On fx-CG 50: F1: CPU @ 116 MHz, BFC @ 58 MHz [Default speed] F2: CPU @ 58 MHz, BFC @ 29 MHz [fx-CG 10/20 default] F3: CPU @ 94 MHz, BFC @ 47 MHz [Clearly slow: F2 < F3 < F1] F4: CPU @ 232 MHz, BFC @ 58 MHz [Fastest CPU option] F5: CPU @ 189 MHz, BFC @ 94 MHz [Fastest bus option] */ CLOCK_SPEED_F1 = 1, CLOCK_SPEED_F2 = 2, CLOCK_SPEED_F3 = 3, CLOCK_SPEED_F4 = 4, CLOCK_SPEED_F5 = 5, /* The default clock speed is always Ftune's F1 */ CLOCK_SPEED_DEFAULT = CLOCK_SPEED_F1,
}
```

If you want to faithfully save and restore the clock state while properly handling clock speeds that are not Ftune/PTune’s defaults, you can get a full copy of the settings.

WARNING: Applying random settings with cpg\_set\_overclock\_setting() might damage your calculator!

```c
struct cpg_overclock_setting
{
  uint32_t FLLFRQ, FRQCR;
  uint32_t CS0BCR, CS2BCR, CS3BCR, CS5aBCR;
  uint32_t CS0WCR, CS2WCR, CS3WCR, CS5aWCR;
}
```

### `cpu_getSR`

[Section titled “cpu\_getSR”](#cpu_getsr)

Read and write the SR register. When writing, only “permanent” bits are set: MD, RB, BL, DSP, IMASK are set. M, Q, S and T are not set to preserve the behavior of ongoing divisions and tests. You can change T with (sett) and (clrt). RC, DMY, DMX and DF are not set: use (setrc), (setdmx), (setdmy), and (clrdmxy). DF is preserved for old-style (setrc) loops to work.

```c
cpu_sr_t cpu_getSR(void)
```

### `sleep`

[Section titled “sleep”](#sleep)

sleep(): Put the processor to sleep

This function uses the \[sleep] instruction to put the processor in sleep mode. This allows reduced energy consumption while waiting for interrupts.

In some certain situations, sleeping would block the process that is being waited for (generally when on-chip memory is involved). When this occurs, this function will not sleep at all and instead return instantly.

The indented use for sleep() is *always* in some sort of loop, as there is no guarantee about time or interrupts elapsed before this function returns.

```c
void sleep(void)
```

***

### `sleep_block`

[Section titled “sleep\_block”](#sleep_block)

sleep\_block(): Block processor sleep

This function blocks processor sleep until sleep\_unblock() is called. The driver maintains a counter of the number of blocking sources, therefore it is important that *every* sleep\_block() is followed by a sleep\_unblock().

```c
void sleep_block(void)
```

***

### `sleep_unblock`

[Section titled “sleep\_unblock”](#sleep_unblock)

```c
void sleep_unblock(void)
```

# Defs: GINT_CALL

> Indirect calls

Unofficial documentation

Community-written docs, valid for the ClassPad port only, possibly slightly outdated. They will be replaced by the official gint documentation once it is published.

The following types and functions can be used to create “indirect function calls”: function calls that are executed several times or a long time after they are created. This is useful for callbacks, where you set up a function to be called when an event occurs. The function and its argument are kept in the call object until the event occurs, at which point the call is realized.

## Functions

[Section titled “Functions”](#functions)

### `gint_call`

[Section titled “gint\_call”](#gint_call)

gint\_call(): Perform an indirect call

```c
static GINLINE int gint_call(gint_call_t cb) { int (*f)(int r4, int r5, int r6, int r7) = (decltype(f))cb.function; int (*f)(int r4, int r5, int r6, int r7) = cb.function; gint_call_arg_t *args = cb.args; return f ? f(args[0].i, args[1].i, args[2].i, args[3].i) : -1; }
```

***

## Macros

[Section titled “Macros”](#macros)

### `POINTER`

[Section titled “POINTER”](#pointer)

Pointers to most common types, in all possible cv-qualifications

```c
#define POINTER ((type, name)) \
  type *name; \
  type const *name ## _c; \
  type volatile *name ## _v; \
  type volatile const *name ## _cv;
```

### `GINT_CALL`

[Section titled “GINT\_CALL”](#gint_call-1)

GINT\_CALL(): Build an indirect call from function and arguments

This macro builds an indirect call (of type gint\_call\_t). Indirect calls are used in various APIs (timers, RTC, DMA, USB…) to notify the program of events that are caused by the hardware instead of the program.

The calls are often made asynchronously, which means that the function setting up the call finishes first, and then the call is made later while some other part of the program is running. This is tricky, because in order to perform the call:

The code and arguments must still exist, even though the function that provided them has returned long ago; The call ABI is lost as soon as we store parameters instead of syntactically performing a call in the code.

For the first issue, the caller has to make sure that every pointer that is passed to the call will still be valid when the call is made; in particular, pointers to variables on the stack can ony be used if the call is guaranteed to be made before the function ends (eg. if there is a synchronous wait in the function).

For the second issue, gint’s indirect call mechanism guarantees ABI compatibility by restricting the arguments that can be passed to the callback.

Only arguments that fit into registers can be passed. In practice, this mostly excludes 64-bit integers, double floating-point values, and custom structures. This way, there is a somewhat solid guarantee that the callback function will take arguments in r4…r7. Only up to 4 arguments can be passed. Only values of the types listed in gint\_call\_arg\_t can be passed.

If you need to work around one of these limitations, pass a pointer to a structure containing your arguments (if the call is invoked after the current function ends, make the structure static or global).

If you need to pass a char or a short, cast to an int and have the function take an int. If you need to pass a pointer to a type not listed in gint\_call\_arg\_t (such as a structure), cast it to (void \*); the function can still take a pointer to the custom type as argument.

If the conditions for the arguments to work are not met, the compiler will emit on of these two errors:

error: static assertion failed: “GINT\_CALL: too many arguments (maximum 4)” -> This is emitted if you have more than 4 arguments. error: cast to union type from type not present in union -> This is emitted if you pass a parameter of an invalid type.

```c
#define GINT_CALL ((func, ...)) \
  ((gint_call_t){ .function = (void *)func, .args = { \
    __VA_OPT__(GINT_CALL_ARGS1(__VA_ARGS__)) \
  }})
```

### `GINT_CALL_ARG`

[Section titled “GINT\_CALL\_ARG”](#gint_call_arg)

Kind of ugly but I don’t have super cool templated logic right now. TODO: Allow any 4-byte type using C++ magic.

```c
#define GINT_CALL_ARG ((expr)) (gint_call_arg_t)(expr)
```

### `GINT_CALL_NULL`

[Section titled “GINT\_CALL\_NULL”](#gint_call_null)

GINT\_CALL\_NULL: Empty function call

```c
#define GINT_CALL_NULL ((gint_call_t){ .function = NULL, .args = {} })
```

### `GINT_CALL_FLAG`

[Section titled “GINT\_CALL\_FLAG”](#gint_call_flag)

GINT\_CALL\_FLAG(): Build an indirect call to an odd address

This is used as a workaround to have an extra flag in gint\_call\_t structures without altering their size and exploits the fact that SuperH code has to be aligned on even addresses. It is up to the caller to notice the presence of the flag and realign the address properly.

This flag is currently only checked by gint\_inth\_callback to specify that the called function will take the interrupt context as its first argument.

```c
#define GINT_CALL_FLAG ((func, ...)) \
  GINT_CALL((void*)((uint32_t)(func) | 1), __VA_ARGS__)
```

```c
#define GINT_CALL_ARGS1 ((a1, ...)) \
  GINT_CALL_ARG(a1), __VA_OPT__(GINT_CALL_ARGS2(__VA_ARGS__))
#define GINT_CALL_ARGS2 ((a2, ...)) \
  GINT_CALL_ARG(a2), __VA_OPT__(GINT_CALL_ARGS3(__VA_ARGS__))
#define GINT_CALL_ARGS3 ((a3, ...)) \
  GINT_CALL_ARG(a3), __VA_OPT__(GINT_CALL_ARGS4(__VA_ARGS__))
#define GINT_CALL_ARGS4 ((a4, ...)) \
  ({ __VA_OPT__(_Static_assert(0, \
    "GINT_CALL: too many arguments (maximum 4)");) \
  GINT_CALL_ARG(a4); })
```

# Display: fx-CG 50

> fx-CG 50 rendering functions

Unofficial documentation

Community-written docs, valid for the ClassPad port only, possibly slightly outdated. They will be replaced by the official gint documentation once it is published.

This module covers rendering functions specific to the fx-CG 50. In addition to triple-buffering management, this mainly includes image manipulation tools as well as the very versatile dimage\_effect() and dsubimage\_effect() functions that support high-performance image rendering with a number of geometric and color effects.

The fx-CG OS restricts the display to a 384x216 rectangle rougly around the center, leaving margins on three sides. However, gint configures the display to use the full 396x224 surface!

## Functions

[Section titled “Functions”](#functions)

### `dsetvram`

[Section titled “dsetvram”](#dsetvram)

dsetvram(): Control video RAM address and triple buffering

Normal rendering under gint uses double-buffering: there is one image displayed on the screen and one in memory, in a region called the video RAM (VRAM). The application draws frames in the VRAM then sends them to the screen only when they are finished, using dupdate().

On fx-CG, sending frames with dupdate() is a common bottleneck because it takes about 11 ms. Fortunately, while the DMA is sending the frame to the display, the CPU is available to do work in parallel. This function sets up triple buffering (ie. a second VRAM) so that the CPU can start working on the next frame while the DMA is sending the current one.

However, experience shows minimal performance improvements, because writing to main RAM does not parallelize with DMA transfers. Since gint 2.8, this is no longer the default, and the memory for the extra VRAM is instead available via malloc().

VRAMs must be contiguous, 32-aligned, (2*396*224)-byte buffers with 32 bytes of extra data on each side (ie. 32 bytes into a 32-aligned buffer of size 177472).

@main Main VRAM area, used alone if \[secondary] is NULL @secondary Additional VRAM area, enables triple buffering if non-NULL

```c
void dsetvram(uint16_t *main, uint16_t *secondary)
```

***

### `dgetvram`

[Section titled “dgetvram”](#dgetvram)

dgetvram() - Get VRAM addresses Returns the VRAM buffer addresses used to render on fx-CG 50.

```c
void dgetvram(uint16_t **main, uint16_t **secondary)
```

***

### `gint_vrambackup_encode`

[Section titled “gint\_vrambackup\_encode”](#gint_vrambackup_encode)

Encode the VRAM contents between \[in\_start] and \[in\_end] at \[output]. While \[\*in\_end] is excluded from the encoding, it will be modified temporarily to serve as bounds check, so it must not be accessed asynchronously during the encoding. The size of the output is not known but is at most the distance between in\_end and in\_start in bytes. Setting output = in\_start to compress in-place is supported. Returns the end pointer after encoding.

```c
uint8_t *gint_vrambackup_encode( uint8_t *output, uint16_t *in_start, uint16_t *in_end)
```

***

### `gint_vrambackup_get`

[Section titled “gint\_vrambackup\_get”](#gint_vrambackup_get)

Get the pointer to the encoded VRAM backup created at load time. If \[size] is not NULL, sets the size in \[\*size]. The pointer is heap allocated and remains owned by gint.

```c
void *gint_vrambackup_get(int *size)
```

***

### `gint_vrambackup_show`

[Section titled “gint\_vrambackup\_show”](#gint_vrambackup_show)

Decode the load-time VRAM backup back to VRAM.

```c
void gint_vrambackup_show(void)
```

### `C_RGB`

[Section titled “C\_RGB”](#c_rgb)

RGB color maker. Takes three channels of value 0..31 each (the extra bit of green is not used).

```c
#define C_RGB ((r,g,b)) (((r) << 11) | ((g) << 6) | (b))
```

```c
#define DWIDTH 320
#define DHEIGHT 528
```

# Display

> Drawing functions

Unofficial documentation

Community-written docs, valid for the ClassPad port only, possibly slightly outdated. They will be replaced by the official gint documentation once it is published.

This module covers the drawing functions that are common to fx9860g and fxcg50. Platform-specific definitions are found in \<gint/display-fx.h> and \<gint/display-cg.h>.

## Functions

[Section titled “Functions”](#functions)

### `dupdate`

[Section titled “dupdate”](#dupdate)

```c
void dupdate(void)
```

***

### `dupdate_set_hook`

[Section titled “dupdate\_set\_hook”](#dupdate_set_hook)

dupdate\_set\_hook(): Define a function to be called after each dupdate()

This functions configures the update hook, which is called after each dupdate() has sent VRAM to the display (but before VRAMs are switched when triple-buffering is used on fx-CG 50).

The hook is mostly useful to send a copy of the frame to another medium, typically through a USB connection to a projector-style application. See usb\_fxlink\_videocapture() in \<gint/usb-ff-bulk.h> for an example.

The function is an indirect call; create one with the GINT\_CALL() macro from \<gint/defs/call.h>. Pass GINT\_CALL\_NULL to disable the feature.

@function Indirect call to perform after each dupdate().

```c
void dupdate_set_hook(gint_call_t function)
```

***

### `dupdate_get_hook`

[Section titled “dupdate\_get\_hook”](#dupdate_get_hook)

dupdate\_get\_hook(): Get a copy of the dupdate() hook

```c
gint_call_t dupdate_get_hook(void)
```

***

### `dclear`

[Section titled “dclear”](#dclear)

dclear(): Fill the screen with a single color

This function clears the screen by painting all the pixels in a single color. It is optimized for opaque colors; on fx-CG 50, it uses dma\_memset() to fill in the VRAM.

Typical running time without overclock: fx-9860G SH3: 70 µs fx-9860G SH4: 15 µs fx-CG 50: 2.5 ms (full-screen drect() is about 6 ms)

On fx9860g, use drect() if you need operators that modify existing pixels instead of replacing them such as invert.

@color fx-9860G: white light\* dark\* black fx-CG 50: Any R5G6B5 color

: When the gray engine is on, see dgray().

```c
void dclear(color_t color)
```

***

### `drect`

[Section titled “drect”](#drect)

drect(): Fill a rectangle of the screen This functions applies a color or an operator to a rectangle defined by two points (x1 y1) and (x2 y2). Both are included in the rectangle.

@x1 @y1 Top-left rectangle corner (included) @x2 @y2 Bottom-right rectangle corner (included) @color fx-9860G: white light\* dark\* black none invert lighten\* darken\* fx-CG 50: Any R5G6B5 color, C\_NONE or C\_INVERT

: When the gray engine is on, see dgray().

```c
void drect(int x1, int y1, int x2, int y2, int color)
```

***

### `drect_border`

[Section titled “drect\_border”](#drect_border)

drect\_border(): Rectangle with border This function draws a rectangle with an inner border. The border width must be smaller than half the width and half the height.

@x1 @y1 @x2 @y2 Top-left and bottom-right rectangle corners (included) @fill\_color Center color (same values as drect() are allowed) @border\_width Amount of pixels reserved for the border on each side @border\_color Border color (same values as drect() are allowed)

```c
void drect_border(int x1, int y1, int x2, int y2, int fill_color, int border_width, int border_color)
```

***

### `dpixel`

[Section titled “dpixel”](#dpixel)

dpixel(): Change a pixel’s color

Paints the selected pixel with an opaque color or applies an operator to a pixel. Setting pixels individually is a slow method for rendering. Other functions that draw lines, rectangles, images or text will take advantage of possible optimizations to make the rendering faster, so prefer using them when they apply.

On fx-9860G, if an operator such as invert is used, the result will depend on the current color of the pixel.

@x @y Coordinates of the pixel to repaint @color fx-9860G: white light\* dark\* black none invert lighten\* darken\* fx-CG 50: Any R5G6B5 color, C\_NONE or C\_INVERT

: When the gray engine is on, see dgray().

```c
void dpixel(int x, int y, int color)
```

***

### `dgetpixel`

[Section titled “dgetpixel”](#dgetpixel)

dgetpixel(): Get a pixel’s color Returns the current color of any pixel in the VRAM. This function ignores the rendering window. Returns -1 if (x,y) is out of bounds.

```c
int dgetpixel(int x, int y)
```

***

### `dline`

[Section titled “dline”](#dline)

dline(): Render a straight line

This function draws a line using a Bresenham-style algorithm. Please note that dline() may not render lines exactly like Bdisp\_DrawLineVRAM().

dline() has optimizations for horizontal and vertical lines. The speedup for horizontal lines is about x2 on fx-CG 50 and probably about x30 on fx-9860G. Vertical lines have a smaller speedup.

dline() is currently not able to clip arbitrary lines without calculating all the pixels, so drawing a line from (-1e6,0) to (1e6,395) will work but will be very slow.

@x1 @y1 @x2 @y2 Endpoints of the line (both included). @color Line color (same values as dpixel() are allowed)

```c
void dline(int x1, int y1, int x2, int y2, int color)
```

***

### `dhline`

[Section titled “dhline”](#dhline)

dhline(): Full-width horizontal line This function draws a horizontal line from the left end of the screen to the right end, much like the Basic command “Horizontal”.

@y Line number @color Line color (same values as dline() are allowed)

```c
void dhline(int y, int color)
```

***

### `dvline`

[Section titled “dvline”](#dvline)

dvline(): Full-height vertical line This function draws a vertical line from the top end of the screen to the bottom end, much like the Basic command “Vertical”.

@x Column number @color Line color (same values as dline() are allowed)

```c
void dvline(int x, int color)
```

***

### `dcircle`

[Section titled “dcircle”](#dcircle)

dcircle(): Circle with border

This function renders a circle defined by its middle point (xm, ym) and a radius r. The border and fill can be set separately. This function uses Bresenham’s algorithm and only renders circles of odd diameter; if you want an even diameter, use dellipse() with a bounding box.

@xm @ym Coordinates of center @r Radius (integer, >= 0) @fill\_color Color of the disc inside the circle, C\_NONE to disable @border\_color Color of the circle itself, C\_NONE to disable

```c
void dcircle(int xm, int ym, int r, int fill_color, int border_color)
```

***

### `dellipse`

[Section titled “dellipse”](#dellipse)

dellipse(): Ellipse with border

This function renders a non-rotated ellipse, defined by its bounding box. The border and fill can be set separately. The border is as 1-pixel thin border given by Bresenham’s algorithm.

To render an ellipse from its center coordinates (x,y) and semi-major/minor axes a/b, use dellipse(x-a, y-b, x+a, y+b, fill\_color, border\_color).

@x1 @y1 @x2 @y2 Ellipse’s bounding box (both bounds included, like drect()) @fill\_color Color of the surface inside the ellipse, C\_NONE to disable @border\_color Color of the ellipse itself, C\_NONE to disable

```c
void dellipse(int x1, int y1, int x2, int y2, int fill_color, int border_color)
```

***

### `dpoly`

[Section titled “dpoly”](#dpoly)

dpoly(): Render an arbitrary polygon

Renders the polygon defined by vertices (x\[i], y\[i]) for 0 < i < N. A fill color and border color can be specified separately. For filling, N must be at least 3. For border, N must be at least 2.

Note: this is a fairly slow function, not designed for rendering triangles in 3D games. There are faster methods for that.

@x @y Arrays of vertex coordinates @N Number of vertices (length of x and y) @fill\_color Color of the polygon’s interior, C\_NONE to disable @border\_color Color of the polygon’s border, C\_NONE to disable

```c
void dpoly(int const *x, int const *y, int N, int fill_color, int border_color)
```

***

### `dfont`

[Section titled “dfont”](#dfont)

dfont(): Set the default font for text rendering

This function changes the default font for text rendering; this affects dtext\_opt(), dtext() and the related functions. If the specified font is NULL, gint’s default font is used instead.

This function returns the previously configured font. Normally you want to restore it after you’re done so as to not affect ambiant calls to text rendering functions. It would look like this:

font\_t const \*old\_font = dfont(new\_font); // Do the text rendering… dfont(old\_font);

@font Font to use for subsequent text rendering calls Returns the previously configured font.

```c
font_t const *dfont(font_t const *font)
```

***

### `dfont_default`

[Section titled “dfont\_default”](#dfont_default)

dfont\_default(): Get gint’s default font

On fx-9860G, the default font is a 5x7 font very close to the system’s. On fx-CG 50, the default font is an original, proportional 8x9 font.

```c
font_t const *dfont_default(void)
```

***

### `dsize`

[Section titled “dsize”](#dsize)

dsize(): Get the width and height of rendered text

This function computes the size that the given string would take up if rendered with a certain font. If you specify a NULL font, the currently configured font will be used; this is different from dfont(), which uses gint’s default font when NULL is passed.

Note that the height of each glyph is not stored in the font, only the maximum. Usually this is what you want because vertically-centered strings must have the same baseline regardless of their contents. So the height set by dsize() is the same for all strings and only depends on the font.

The height is computed in constant time, and the width in linear time. If the third argument is NULL, this function returns in constant time.

@str String whose size must be evaluated @font Font to use; if NULL, defaults to the current font @w @h Set to the width and height of the rendered text, may be NULL

```c
void dsize(char const *str, font_t const *font, int *w, int *h)
```

***

### `dnsize`

[Section titled “dnsize”](#dnsize)

dnsize(): Get the width and height of rendered text, with character limit

This function is similar to dsize(), but stops after (size) bytes If (size < 0), there is no limit and this function is identical to dsize().

@str String whose size must be evaluated @size Maximum number of bytes to read from (str) @font Font to use; if NULL, defaults to the current font @w @h Set to the width and height of the rendered text, may be NULL

```c
void dnsize(char const *str, int size, font_t const *font, int *w, int *h)
```

***

### `drsize`

[Section titled “drsize”](#drsize)

drsize(): Get width of rendered text with reverse size limit

This function is the opposite of dnsize(). It determines how many characters of (str) can fit into the specified (width), and returns a pointer to the first character after that section. If (w) is non-NULL, it it set to the width of the section, which is typically a couple of pixels smaller than the provided limit.

@str String to read characters from @font Font to use; if NULL, defaults to the current font @width Maximum width @w Set to the width of the rendered text, may be NULL Returns a pointer to first character that doesn’t fit, or end-of-str

```c
char const *drsize(char const *str, font_t const *font, int width, int *w)
```

***

### `dtext_opt`

[Section titled “dtext\_opt”](#dtext_opt)

dtext\_opt(): Display a string of text

Draws some text in the video RAM using the font set with dfont() (or gint’s default if no such font was set). This function has a lot of parameters, see dtext() for a simpler version.

The alignment options specify where (x y) should be relative to the rendered string. The default is halign=DTEXT\_LEFT and valign=DTEXT\_TOP, which means that (x y) is the top-left corder of the rendered string. The different combinations of settings provide 9 positions of (x y) to choose from.

On fx-9860G, due to the particular design of topti, this function performs drastic rendering optimizations using the line structure of the VRAM and renders 5 or 6 characters simultaneously.

This is not a printf()-family function so str cannot contain formats like “%d” and you cannot pass additional arguments. See dprint\_opt() and dprint() for that.

@x @y Coordinates of the anchor of the rendered string @fg @bg Text color and background color fx-9860G: white light\* dark\* black none invert lighten\* darken\* fx-CG 50: Any R5G6B6 color, or C\_NONE @halign Where x should be relative to the rendered string @valign Where y should be relative to the rendered string @str String to display @size Maximum number of bytes to display (negative for no limit)

```c
void dtext_opt(int x, int y, int fg, int bg, int halign, int valign, char const *str, int size)
```

***

### `dtext`

[Section titled “dtext”](#dtext)

dtext(): Simple version of dtext\_opt() with defaults Calls dtext\_opt() with bg=C\_NONE, halign=DTEXT\_LEFT and valign=DTEXT\_TOP.

```c
void dtext(int x, int y, int fg, char const *str)
```

***

### `dprint_opt`

[Section titled “dprint\_opt”](#dprint_opt)

dprint\_opt(): Display a formatted string

This function is exactly like dtext\_opt(), but accepts printf-like formats with arguments. See \<gint/std/stdio.h> for a detailed view of what this format supports. For example:

dprint\_opt(x, y, fg, bg, halign, valign, “A=%d B=%d”, A, B);

```c
void dprint_opt(int x, int y, int fg, int bg, int halign, int valign, char const *format, ...)
```

***

### `dprint`

[Section titled “dprint”](#dprint)

dprint(): Simple version of dprint\_op() with defaults Calls dprint\_opt() with bg=C\_NONE, halign=DTEXT\_LEFT and valign=DTEXT\_TOP

```c
void dprint(int x, int y, int fg, char const *format, ...)
```

***

### `dimage`

## Types

[Section titled “Types”](#types)

font\_t: Font data encoded for topti

```c
typedef struct
{
  /* Font name (NUL-terminated), NULL if no title */ char const *name;
  /* Font shape flags */ uint bold :1;
  uint italic :1;
  uint serif :1;
  uint mono :1;
  uint :3;
  /* Whether data is variable-length (proportional font) */ uint prop :1;
  /* Line height */ uint8_t line_height;
  /* Storage height */ uint8_t data_height;
  /* Number of Unicode blocks */ uint8_t block_count;
  /* Number of total glyphs */ uint32_t glyph_count;
  /* Character spacing (usually 1) */ uint8_t char_spacing;
  /* Distance between the y positions for two consecutive lines. This is an informative metric for text wrapping tools, not used by dtext() and other standard functions that always write a single line. */ uint8_t line_distance;
  uint :16;
  struct
  {
    /* Unicode point of first character in block */ uint start :20;
    /* Length of block */ uint length :12;
  }
  *blocks;
  /* Raw glyph data */ uint32_t *data;
  union
  {
    /* For monospaced fonts */ struct
    {
      /* Width of glyphs */ uint16_t width;
      /* Storage size, in longwords, of each glyph */ uint16_t storage_size;
    }
    ;
    /* For proportional fonts */ struct
    {
      /* Storage index to find glyphs quickly */ uint16_t *glyph_index;
      /* Width of each individual glyph */ uint8_t *glyph_width;
    }
    ;
  }
  ;
}
font_t
```

## Data structures

[Section titled “Data structures”](#data-structures)

dmode: Rendering mode settings

This structure indicates the current window settings. Rendering is limited to the rectangle spanning from (left,top) included, to (right,bottom) excluded. The default is from (0,0) to (DWIDTH,DHEIGHT).

```c
struct dwindow
{
  int left, top;
  int right, bottom;
}
```

dwindow\_set(): Set the rendering window

This function changes \[dwindow] settings to limit rendering to a sub-surface of the VRAM. Note that this doesn’t change the coordinate system; the pixel at (DWIDTH/2, DHEIGHT/2) is always in the middle of the screen regardless of the window setting. However, it might be masked out by the window.

Returns the old dwindow settings (if it needs to be restored later).

```c
struct dwindow dwindow_set(struct dwindow new_mode)
```

Alignment settings for dtext\_opt() and dprint\_opt(). Combining a vertical and a horizontal alignment option specifies where a given point (x,y) should be relative to the rendered string.

```c
enum
{
  /* Horizontal settings: default in dtext() is DTEXT_LEFT */ DTEXT_LEFT = 0, DTEXT_CENTER = 1, DTEXT_RIGHT = 2, /* Vertical settings: default in dtext() is DTEXT_TOP */ DTEXT_TOP = 0, DTEXT_MIDDLE = 1, DTEXT_BOTTOM = 2,
}
```

Option values for dsubimage()

```c
enum
{
  /* No option */ DIMAGE_NONE = 0x00, /* Disable clipping, ie. adjustments to the specified subrectangle and screen location such that any part that overflows from the image or the screen is ignored. Slightly faster. */ DIMAGE_NOCLIP = 0x01,
}
```

# DMA

> Direct Memory Access for efficient data transfer

Unofficial documentation

Community-written docs, valid for the ClassPad port only, possibly slightly outdated. They will be replaced by the official gint documentation once it is published.

## Functions

[Section titled “Functions”](#functions)

### `dma_transfer_async`

[Section titled “dma\_transfer\_async”](#dma_transfer_async)

dma\_transfer\_async(): Perform an asynchronous DMA data transfer

This function starts a DMA data transfer and returns immediately. The provided callback will be invoked once the transfer is finish. You can also call dma\_transfer\_wait() to wait until the transfer completes. You can create a callback with GINT\_CALL() or pass GINT\_CALL\_NULL.

@channel DMA channel (0..5) @size Transfer size @blocks Number of blocks (transferred memory = size \* blocks) @src Source pointer, must be aligned with transfer size @src\_mode Source address mode @dst Destination address, must be aligned with transfer size @dst\_mode Destination address mode @callback Function to invoke when the transfer finishes -> Returns true on success.

```c
bool dma_transfer_async(int channel, dma_size_t size, uint blocks, void const *src, dma_address_t src_mode, void *dst, dma_address_t dst_mode, gint_call_t callback)
```

***

### `dma_transfer_wait`

[Section titled “dma\_transfer\_wait”](#dma_transfer_wait)

dma\_transfer\_wait(): Wait for an asynchronous transfer to finish @channel DMA channel (0..5)

```c
void dma_transfer_wait(int channel)
```

***

### `dma_transfer_sync`

[Section titled “dma\_transfer\_sync”](#dma_transfer_sync)

dma\_transfer\_sync(): Perform an synchronous DMA data transfer Like dma\_transfer\_async(), but only returns once the transfer completes.

```c
bool dma_transfer_sync(int channel, dma_size_t size, uint blocks, void const *src, dma_address_t src_mode, void *dst, dma_address_t dst_mode)
```

***

### `dma_transfer_atomic`

[Section titled “dma\_transfer\_atomic”](#dma_transfer_atomic)

dma\_transfer\_atomic(): Perform a data transfer without interrupts

This function performs a transfer much like dma\_transfer\_sync(), but doesn’t use interrupts and actively waits for the transfer to finish. Not using interrupts is a bad design idea for a majority of programs, and is only ever needed to display panic messages inside exception handlers.

```c
void dma_transfer_atomic(int channel, dma_size_t size, uint blocks, void const *src, dma_address_t src_mode, void *dst, dma_address_t dst_mode)
```

***

### `__attribute__`

### `dma_memset`

[Section titled “dma\_memset”](#dma_memset)

dma\_memset(): Fast 32-aligned memset

This function is your typical memset(), except that the destination and size must be 32-aligned, and that the pattern is 4 bytes instead of one. It is replicated to 32 bytes then used to fill the destination area. This 4-byte fixed size may be lifted in future versions.

This function cannot be used with virtualized (P0) addresses.

@dst Destination address (32-aligned) @pattern 4-byte pattern to fill @dst @size Sie of destination area (32-aligned)

```c
void *dma_memset(void *dst, uint32_t pattern, size_t size)
```

***

### `dma_memcpy`

[Section titled “dma\_memcpy”](#dma_memcpy)

dma\_memcpy(): Fast 32-aligned memcpy

This function works exactly like memcpy(), but it expects 32-aligned source, destination, and size, and uses the DMA to efficiently copy.

This function cannot be used with virtualized (P0) addresses.

@dst Destination address (32-aligned) @dst Source addresss (32-aligned) @size Size of region (32-aligned)

```c
void *dma_memcpy(void * __restrict dst, const void * __restrict src, size_t size)
```

## Macros

### `GINT_DECLARE_DRIVER`

[Section titled “GINT\_DECLARE\_DRIVER”](#gint_declare_driver)

GINT\_DECLARE\_DRIVER(): Declare a driver to the kernel

Use this macro to declare a driver by passing it the name of a gint\_driver\_t structure. This macro moves the structure to the .gint.drivers.\* sections, which are automatically traversed at startup.

The level argument represents the priority level: lower numbers mean that drivers will be loaded sooner. This numbering allows a primitive form of dependency for drivers. You need to specify a level which is strictly higher than the level of all the drivers you depend on.

The level number *MUST HAVE EXACTLY 2 DIGITS*, as it is used as a string in the section name and the linker then sorts by name. If your driver has a level lower than 10, you must add a leading 0.

```c
#define GINT_DECLARE_DRIVER ((level, name)) \
  GSECTION(".gint.drivers." #level) GVISIBLE extern gint_driver_t name;
```

### `gint_driver_count`

[Section titled “gint\_driver\_count”](#gint_driver_count)

Number of drivers in the (gint\_drivers) array

```c
#define gint_driver_count (()) \
  ((gint_driver_t *)&gint_drivers_end - (gint_driver_t *)&gint_drivers)
```

## Types

[Section titled “Types”](#types)

```c
typedef struct
{
  /* Driver name */ char const *name;
  /* General constructor, is called before any interaction with the driver. This can be used to adjust settings based on detected hardware. */ void (*constructor)(void);
  // Foreign calls /* Foreign unbind: separate the hardware from the OS driver. If NULL, the OS driver is always considered idle. */ void (*funbind)(void);
  // "Hypervisor" calls /* Determine whether the device is powered. If NULL, the device is assumed to be permanently powered. */ bool (*hpowered)(void);
  /* Power on the device;
  this should allow register access to save the peripheral state, with minimal state changes. Cannot be NULL if hpowered() can return false. */ void (*hpoweron)(void);
  /* Power off the device;
  cannot be NULL if hpowered() can return false. */ void (*hpoweroff)(void);
  /* Save the hardware state;
  the (state) pointer points to a 4-aligned region of (state_size) bytes. */ void (*hsave)(void *state);
  /* Restore a hardware state previously saved by hsave(). */ void (*hrestore)(void const *state);
  // Standard calls /* Bind the driver to acquire control of the device. May be NULL. */ void (*bind)(void);
  /* Unbind the driver from the hardware. Usually sleeps until processes that block world switches terminate, like bind(). May be NULL. */ void (*unbind)(void);
  /* Initialize the hardware for the driver to work in gint. Usually installs interrupt handlers and configures registers. May be NULL. */ void (*configure)(void);
  /* Size of the peripheral's hardware state (assumed 4-aligned) */ uint16_t state_size;
  /* Initial flags */ uint8_t flags;
}
gint_driver_t
```

gint\_world\_t: World state capture

The world state is a copy of the (almost) complete hardware state, which can be used to switch between several kernels running in parallel on the same machine. gint runs in a different world than the OS, allowing it to control peripheral modules in ways incompatible with the OS without compromising the stability of either program.

The world state is a sequence of 4-aligned buffers each holding a copy of a module’s state, as saved (and restored) by a driver. It is prefixed with an array of pointers, one for each driver, specifying the driver’s spot within the sequence.

The layout is as follows: An array of (void \*), with one entry per driver, in priority order. Each pointer is to a buffer in the sequence. A sequence of buffers of size (state\_size), rounded up to a multiple of 4 bytes, for each driver in priority order.

The world is returned as a (void \*) array but allocated in one block.

```c
typedef void **gint_world_t
```

```c
}
```
